[therein]; only that they let the Masses go, and whatsoever more is such abomination. As the
visitors also have shown. Doctor Martin Luther's opinion is also that in the parishes, morning
and evening, the scholars be let sing two or three psalms and read a lesson, item the
*Benedictus*, *Magnificat*, *Te Deum laudamus*, *Quicunque vult salvus esse*, [and] the
*Preces*, that they also abide by the Scripture.

The two levels are already here: the **full hours in chapters and convents**, and **two offices
in the parishes**, sung by the school.

**The Wittenberg castle church, 1525.** The order for the All Saints' foundation in the castle
at Wittenberg, where there was no parish, abolishes the Mass there but keeps a full Latin
office. Vespers and Compline are joined: after the *Benedicamus* the psalm *Qui habitat* and the
*Nunc dimittis* are read without tone. Matins has a hymn verse, three psalms and three lessons
from St Paul with three responsories, the *Te Deum*, and Lauds with the *Benedictus*. The little
hours keep their structure, with a lesson from the Gospels in place of the chapter.
**Wittenberg, *Wie es einer zeit mit den ceremonien der kirchen gehalten wirt*, 1525**
(Sehling 1, p. 699):

<!-- doc 147 -->
> Ad primam, terciam, sextam, nonam. Sine deus in adiutorium. Ab hymnis illis consuetis
> incipiatur, post cantetur psalmus beati immaculati etc. et dividatur in has quattuor horas
> more solito cum antiphonis ex psalterio vel de tempore. Post antiphonam loco capituli consueti
> legatur lectio ex evangelistis incipiendo a Matthia, ita ut unum caput dividatur in quattuor
> partes secundum istas quattuor horas […].

At Prime, Terce, Sext [and] None. Without *Deus in adiutorium*. Let it begin with those
customary hymns; after, let the psalm *Beati immaculati* etc. be sung, and let it be divided
among these four hours in the accustomed manner, with antiphons from the psalter or *de
tempore*. After the antiphon, in place of the customary chapter, let a lesson be read from the
evangelists, beginning with Matthew, so that one chapter be divided into four parts according to
these four hours […].

The order is explicit that all this is free: "we will that consciences be not bound by these
things, as if by precept under necessity of salvation" (Sehling 1, p. 699).

#### <a id="s10-4-2"></a>10.4.2 Collegiate churches and cathedrals

**Brandenburg-Ansbach, 1531–1533.** The Ansbach theologians' advice of 1531 lets the canons keep
all seven hours, with only "the evil, offensive and uncertain" removed. It complains that the
hours had been sung "with such haste that no choir heeded or waited for the other".
**Brandenburg-Ansbach-Kulmbach, *Gottesdienstmandat*, 1531** (Sehling 11, p. 312):

<!-- doc 275 -->
> Und bliben inen gleich wol ir horae, das ist tagzeit als mettin, prim, terz, sext, non, vesper
> und complet, wurde allain das bös, ergerlich und ungewis underlassen, welchs doch kain
> gutherziger gotzverstendiger strafen kunde. Nun ist auch meniglich bewust, das die horae von
> inen bisher ganz unordenlich und unfleißig gesungen sind worden mit solcher eil, das kain chor
> auf den andem gemerket und gewartet hat und oft der ander chor angefangen zu singen, ehe jener
> ausgesungen […].

And their hours would yet remain to them, that is, the times of day, as Matins, Prime, Terce,
Sext, None, Vespers and Compline; only the evil, offensive and uncertain would be left out,
which no good-hearted man that understandeth God could blame. Now it is also known to everyone
that the hours have hitherto been sung by them altogether disorderly and carelessly, with such
haste that no choir heeded or waited for the other, and often the second choir began to sing
before the first had finished […].

The *Ordnung singens und lesens bei den Stiften* of 1533 then goes through the Breviary hour by
hour (Sehling 11, pp. 313–316):
- At Matins a whole chapter of the Old Testament is divided into the three lessons, so that the
  Old Testament is read through "in one or two years".
- Lauds is shortened to three psalms a day, each day with its own.
- Prime, Terce, Sext and None keep their hymns and psalms. At Terce a whole chapter of the
  Epistles replaces the chapter, beginning with Acts.
- The *preces* are dropped every day.
- Collects that sound of the saints or of merit are struck out one by one (see
  [Chapter 5](#ch5), [§5.6.6](#s5-6-6)).

**Brandenburg, 1540.** The electoral order of Joachim II keeps the whole Latin choir office in
all chapters, convents and parish churches where it was customary, "according to each
bishopric's Breviary". **Brandenburg, *Kirchen-ordnung* of Joachim II, 1540**
(Sehling 3, pp. 71–72):

<!-- doc 1746 -->
> Der chorgesang sol, wie bisanher, in allen stiften und klöstern, auch den pfarkirchen, wie.
> der gebreuchlich gewesen, latinisch gesungen und gelesen werden, zuvoran, so es de tempore
> ist, da sol nichts nachgelassen werden, es sei metten, prima, tertia, sexta, nona, vesper,
> complet oder was der mehr ist, ein iglichs, wie mans findet, nach seiner rubrica on alle
> leichtfertigkeit. Was aber de sanctis ist, sol von uns und unsern verordneten ubersehen und,
> wo es von nöten, corrigirt werden […]. Sonst sol offentlich in den kirchen gesungen und
> gelesen werden, beide früe und spat, nach eins jeden bistums brevir aus den vorigen
> sangbüchern […].

The choir chant shall, as hitherto, in all chapters and convents, and also in the parish
churches where it hath been customary, be sung and read in Latin; above all, where it is *de
tempore*, nothing shall be omitted, be it Matins, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, Compline or
whatever more there is, each as it is found, according to its rubric, without any lightness. But
what is *de sanctis* shall be looked over by us and those we appoint, and where needful
corrected […]. Otherwise shall be sung and read publicly in the churches, both early and late,
according to each bishopric's Breviary, out of the former choir books […].

**Naumburg cathedral, c. 1541–1543.** The cathedral chapter sent the elector an account of its
daily worship. It keeps every hour and joins them to the evangelical preaching. **Naumburg,
*Gottesdienst-Ordnung in der Domkirche*, 1543 (1541?), printed in Sehling's supplement**
(Sehling 2, p. 596):

<!-- doc 1265 -->
> Morgens in precibus matutinis werden gehalten drei psalm, drei lectiones mit responsoriis de
> tempore und von den festen, welcher historien in der heiligen schrift gegruendet. Unter dem Te
> deum laudamus geschiecht ein sonderlicher puels zu der teuzschen lection. Nach deme Te deum
> laudamus werden gehalten psalmi de laudibus mit dem cantico Zacharie, und concludirt mit der
> collecten de tempore die metten. Darauf wirt gelesen auf teuzschs ein capitel aus der biblien
> mit einem summario und das volk vormanet zum gebete, und mit einem deuzschen gesinge und
> collecten beschlossen. Umb die sechste stunde werden die prime und terz gehalten de tempore
> […]. Umb die neunde stunde werden gehalten sext und nona. Vespertine preces und completorium
> werden zwischen zweien und dreien gehalten.

In the morning, in the morning prayers, are kept three psalms [and] three lessons, with
responsories *de tempore* and of the feasts whose histories are grounded in holy Scripture.
During the *Te Deum laudamus* a special bell is rung for the German lesson. After the *Te Deum
laudamus* are kept the psalms of Lauds with the Canticle of Zachary, and Matins is concluded
with the collect *de tempore*. Thereupon a chapter out of the Bible is read in German with a
summary, and the people are exhorted to prayer, and it is concluded with a German hymn and
collects. About the sixth hour Prime and Terce are kept *de tempore* […]. About the ninth hour
are kept Sext and None. The evening prayers and Compline are kept between two and three.

On Sundays and feasts "the hours, as the morning prayers, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, are kept in
order one after another", and the bell for the sermon and the Lord's Supper is rung under None
(Sehling 2, p. 596).

**Other chapters.** The full Latin cursus is kept, corrected *de tempore*, in:
- **Altenburg castle chapter, 1533**: "the seven hours … and briefly, with only one nocturn", so
  that the canons "go not altogether idle"; the "pure new Litany" replaces the *preces*
  (Sehling 1, p. 515).
- **Goslar, St Simon and Judas, 1534**: Sehling's introduction notes that Widensee "keeps the
  outward form of the office": the canonical hours stay in the choir, the length is not reduced,
  and Latin is kept. Only the Lord's Supper is in German (Sehling 7/2.2, p. 199).
- **Pfalz-Neuburg 1543**: where chapters, convents and parishes sing "some or all of the
  canonical hours, daily or only on certain feasts", they shall continue (Sehling 13, p. 77).
  The Heidelberg chapter of the Holy Spirit followed the same text in 1546 (Sehling 14, p. 91).
- **Quakenbrück, 1543**: Hermann Bonnus's "daily exercise in the Scriptures and in singing
  psalms, for collegiate churches where the Gospel is preached" (Sehling 7/1, p. 229; [§10.6.2](#s10-6-2)).
- **Öhringen 1556**: "the old and young persons of the chapter shall sing them daily in order"
  (Sehling 15, p. 102).
- **Verden cathedral, 1606**: Matins and Vespers on Saturdays, Sundays and feasts, "as the old
  order bringeth with it", with the pure antiphons, psalms, responsories and hymns, ending "with
  the *Benedicamus* or Compline" (Sehling 7/1, p. 153).

#### <a id="s10-4-3"></a>10.4.3 Bugenhagen's order for the remaining canons and monks

**A complete Latin cursus.** Bugenhagen's *Pia ordinatio* (Pomerania 1535) has a full order of
hours "according to the number of the hours hitherto customary". It was made for the monks who
could not leave and for "the canons, who are now of no use to the Church of Christ". It passed
into the Danish order of 1537, the Schleswig-Holstein order of 1542 (in Low German) and
Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel 1543 (Sehling 23, p. 142; 6/1, p. 81). **Pomerania, *Pia ordinatio
caeremoniarum*, 1535** (Sehling 4, p. 349):

<!-- doc 1857 -->
> Eadem plane dicimus de canonicis, qui nullo iam usui sunt ecclesiae Christi. Possunt et ipsi
> residui, si non aliis offitiis necessariis sunt commodi, ita hisce scripturae exercitiis
> cantando pro suo tempore exerceri. Sic vero potest ordinari cantus cum lectionibus (si ita
> placet) secundum numerum horarum hactenus consuetarum: […]

The same we say plainly of the canons, who are now of no use to the Church of Christ. They also
that remain, if they be not fit for other necessary offices, may thus be exercised in these
exercises of Scripture by singing, for their time. And thus may the chant with the lessons be
ordered (if it so please), according to the number of the hours hitherto customary: […]

The order then gives Matins (with Lauds), Prime, Terce, Sext, None and Vespers, and Compline
recited "with a low voice without any tone" ([§10.7.1](#s10-7-1)). Its purpose is stated at the end: the psalms
are to run on from day to day, and the whole Bible is to be read "twice or more in a year", for
the consolation of those "who, hindered by age or otherwise, cannot now take up a better
condition, until they render their spirit to God" (Sehling 4, p. 350).

#### <a id="s10-4-4"></a>10.4.4 The women's convents

**The convents kept the hours longest.** Most surviving women's houses became evangelical
convents, and most of their orders keep the hours, purged and shortened:
- **Nimbschen, 1529** (Katharina von Bora's former convent): on feasts "they shall sing Matins,
  Prime, Terce, Sext etc." (Sehling 1, p. 617).
- **The Leipzig friaries, 1539**: the remaining friars may keep the canonical hours *de tempore*
  "among themselves, yet without bells and with the church doors locked, in quiet"
  (Sehling 1, p. 589). The *Gemeines Fürhalten* of the same visitation allows the religious,
  "until further provision", to "read or sing the seven hours, yet only *de tempore* and what is
  agreeable to God's word, … as a church exercise" (Sehling 1, p. 590).
- **Spandau, 1541**: the nuns' Breviary was examined by the visitors and corrected. They keep
  Matins (three psalms, a chapter divided into three lessons with responsories, the *Te Deum*
  and Lauds), Prime, Terce, Sext and None, and between Prime and Terce one of them reads an
  article of the church order or the catechism aloud in the refectory (Sehling 3, p. 305).
- **The Calenberg convents, 1542**: Lauds only on Sundays and feasts; "Prima, tertia, sexta,
  nona … with the customary psalms, antiphons and collects"; Vespers and Compline "with the
  customary psalms, antiphons, hymns" (Sehling 6/2, p. 851).
- **Frankenberg at Goslar, 1542**: a Latin order in place of the hours, which the nuns "shall do
  freely and not under constraint", without sin "if they keep them less exactly or even leave
  them off altogether" (Sehling 7/2.2, p. 277).
- **The Lüneburg convents, 1555**: all seven hours, with a corrected Breviary (below).
- **Keppel in Nassau, 1570**: all seven hours, in German ([§10.8.2](#s10-8-2)).

**Lüneburg, 1555.** The *Reformatio coenobiorum* of 1555 orders the nuns of the Lüneburg
convents to meet daily for all seven hours, with the chants and lessons corrected. **Lüneburg,
*Reformatio coenobiorum ducatus Luneburgensis*, 1555** (Sehling 6/1, pp. 611–612):

<!-- doc 2009 -->
> Zum dritten sollen die klosterjungfrauen Gott mit lesen und singen loben und ehren und vor die
> zeitliche und ewige wolfart bitten, und derwegen soilen sie alle tage etliche zeit in der
> kirchen zusamenkommen und in den metten, prim, terz, sext, non, vesper und complet die
> christliche gesenge und lectiones de tempore und von den hohen festen, auch de sanctis, doch
> mit der christlichen correction und veranderung, wie die sonderlich beschrieben und verordenet
> sein, singen und lesen.

Thirdly, the convent virgins shall praise and honour God with reading and singing, and pray for
the temporal and eternal welfare; and therefore they shall every day for some time come together
in the church, and in Matins, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers and Compline sing and read the
Christian chants and lessons *de tempore* and of the high feasts, and also *de sanctis*, yet
with the Christian correction and alteration, as the same are specially written down and
ordained.

The "correction" is the *Emendatio Breviarii virginum ordinis Sancti Benedicti in ducatu
Luneburgensi* of the same year, a revised Benedictine Breviary for the nuns. It marks what may
be "read and sung piously" and what may be "omitted without any scruple of conscience"
(Sehling 6/1, p. 624).

**Breslau, 1557.** A report of 1557 on the order of the Breslau churches says that in the
Lutheran city the choralists still sang Little Hours of the medieval type every weekday morning:
"the hours of the Passion of the Lord", and on Fridays "the hours of the Visitation of the
Blessed Virgin Mary", before the Mass (Sehling 3, p. 405).

---

### <a id="s10-5"></a>10.5 Where the system was cut down

#### <a id="s10-5-1"></a>10.5.1 The case against the hours

**"Murmurings".** The sharpest words come from Bugenhagen's *Pia ordinatio*. The monks are to be
taught that Christ alone is their righteousness, and that "those murmurings of the canonical
hours, and long and feigned prayers, are wearyings of the body and vexations of the conscience".
**Pomerania, *Pia ordinatio caeremoniarum*, 1535** (Sehling 4, p. 345):

<!-- doc 1857 -->
> murmura vero illa horarum canonicarum et lougas simulatasque preces esse fatigationes corporum
> et vexationes conscientiarum. Deinde nihil canant aut legant publice, quod non sit ex sacra
> acceptum scriptura, id est ex veteri et novo testamento […].

but that those murmurings of the canonical hours, and long and feigned prayers, are wearyings of
the body and vexations of the conscience. Further, that they sing or read nothing publicly that
is not taken from holy Scripture, that is, from the Old and New Testament […].

Schleswig-Holstein 1542 has the same in Low German: "dat Murrent der tide, dat men nömet Horas
Canonicas" (Sehling 23, p. 131). Yet the same order goes on to give the full cursus ([§10.4.3](#s10-4-3)). The
objection is to the hours as a burden on the conscience, not to the psalms sung in course.

**What "canonical hours" ought to mean.** The Hamburg order of 1529 argues that the hours took
their name from the reading of canonical Scripture. Rightly understood, they would be hours of
lectures on the Bible, "as now in the high school at Wittenberg". **Hamburg, *Kirchenordnung*,
1529** (Sehling 5, p. 493):

<!-- doc 1958 -->
> So hefft me etlike bestemmede stunden des dages gehat, dar inne me gelesen und gehöret hefft
> scripturam canonicam, alse nu in der hogen schole tho Wittenberch. Up de stunde hefft
> canonicus Petrus gelesen canonicam scripturam, up eine andere stunde canonicus Joannes etc.,
> dar van sint solcke bestemmede stunden hore canonice genömet. In welcken so to lesende und
> scrift to utleggende, dat me gelerde pastores unde evangelistas mochte van den tohörers maken,
> were wol recht horas canonicas lesen.

So there were certain appointed hours of the day, wherein canonical Scripture was read and
heard, as now in the high school at Wittenberg. At one hour the canon Peter read the canonical
Scripture, at another hour the canon John, etc.; from this such appointed hours are named *horae
canonicae*. In these so to read and to expound Scripture, that learned pastors and evangelists
might be made of the hearers, were indeed rightly to read the canonical hours.

Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel 1543 repeats the etymology: "these are also *horae canonicae*, the
hours in which canonical Scripture is read and treated" (Sehling 6/1, p. 49).

**"Not burdened with the canonical hours".** Several territorial orders free the chapters and
convents from the hours altogether, and put preaching in their place. **Mecklenburg,
*Kirchenordnung*, 1552** (Sehling 5, p. 196):

<!-- doc 1922 -->
> sollen auch den stiften und klöstern ernstlich befehlen, das sie sich den pfarkirchen
> gleichformig machen, mit predigen, mit der communio und mit andern christlichen ceremonien,
> und mit abthuung der misbreuch, der opfermess, der heiligen anrufung, gelübden und kappen etc.
> Sollen auch nicht mit den horis canonicis beladen sein.

[They] shall also earnestly command the chapters and convents that they make themselves
conformable to the parish churches, with preaching, with the communion and with other Christian
ceremonies, and with the putting away of the abuses, the sacrificial Mass, the invocation of the
saints, vows and cowls, etc. They shall also not be burdened with the canonical hours.

The Lippe order of 1538 has the same words in Low German: "Schollen oick nicht mit den horis
canonicis beladen syn" (Sehling 21, p. 343). The Mecklenburg convent order of 1572 frees the
nuns too: "none of the virgins shall be burdened with the canonical hours *de tempore*", for
true prayer "is not bound to certain times and places" and does not please God "for the sake of
the work, especially when it is babbled without understanding in the Latin unknown tongue"
(Sehling 5, p. 257). In its place it sets a daily German office of its own ([§10.8.2](#s10-8-2)).

**Hours displaced by preaching.** Where the old clergy kept their hours beside the evangelical
preachers, the orders protect the sermon:
- **Herford 1532**: while there is preaching, "no priests shall sing or read their hours in any
  church" (Sehling 21, p. 170).
- **Zwickau 1545**: "the singing of the hours in the hospital of St Margaret shall be
  abolished". The hospital preacher is instead to sing "a psalm or spiritual song" daily with
  the poor and read them a lesson from the Old or New Testament (Sehling 1, p. 725).

#### <a id="s10-5-2"></a>10.5.2 Two offices, sung by the school

**Bugenhagen's argument.** The commonest Lutheran form is Luther's 1526 pattern: Matins and
Vespers, sung daily by the Latin school. Bugenhagen's Braunschweig order of 1528 gives the
reason in terms that recur at Hamburg 1529 and Lübeck 1531. The old school custom of singing
psalms, antiphons and responsories helped learned men "to learning and to memory". It had been
spoiled only where "the canonical hours and other things without end" were sung and left to
"drunken choirboys". **Braunschweig, *Kirchenordnung*, 1528** (Sehling 6/1, p. 399):

<!-- doc 1983 -->
> Vele, de gelert synt, möten bekennen, dat id en tor lere unde tor memorie geholpen hefft, dat
> se in der jöget mosten singen psalme unde etlike antiphen unde responsoria etc., welk ock
> plach mit guder meticheit gewönlick syn in kleynen steden unde ock in groten, alse noch, dar
> me nicht singet horas canonicas unde andere dink, des neyn ende is, dat ock vordretlick is
> geworden den presteren unde bevalen den drunkenen chorschöleren. Darumme wille wy sulke
> nutticheit unsen kynderen ock hebben, dat se avent unde morgen singen unde lesen alle dage,
> welk me plecht to nömen vesper unde metten.

Many that are learned must confess that it hath helped them to learning and to memory that in
their youth they had to sing psalms and certain antiphons and responsories etc., which also was
wont to be customary with good measure in small towns and also in great ones (as it yet is where
they sing not the canonical hours and other things whereof there is no end), which also became
irksome to the priests, and [was] committed to the drunken choirboys. Therefore we will have
such profit for our children also, that they sing and read evening and morning every day, which
is wont to be named Vespers and Matins.

**Enough for a parish church.** Bugenhagen's Pomeranian order of 1535 says the same in its own
terms. The boys sing Latin psalms and lessons with the *Benedictus* in the morning, and psalms,
lessons, a hymn and the *Magnificat* in the afternoon, each for no more than a quarter of an
hour. **Pomerania, *Kirchenordnung*, 1535** (Sehling 4, p. 342):

<!-- doc 1856 -->
> An solckeme singende unde ceremonien is idt genoch vor de parrekercken, dat me nene horas
> canonicos (!) eder andere meer bedarf. Me schal de kindere des werkeldages in der kercken
> nicht över ein verndel van der stunde laten singen, dat se sick alse mit luste gewonnen to der
> hiligen schrift, unde ljkewol dar mede nicht vorsümet werden in erer scholekunst […].

With such singing and ceremonies it is enough for the parish churches, so that no canonical
hours (!) or anything more be needed. On working days the children shall not be let sing in the
church above a quarter of an hour, that they so with delight grow used to holy Scripture, and
yet be not hindered thereby in their school learning […].

**The towns.** Matins and Vespers in this form, or Saturday and Sunday Vespers with Sunday
Matins, are the rule in the town orders:
- Wittenberg 1533 (Sehling 1, pp. 701–705);
- Saxony 1539 and 1580 (Sehling 1, pp. 564, 368);
- Senftenberg 1555 (Sehling 1, pp. 671–672);
- Prussia 1568 (Sehling 4, pp. 74–75);
- Hoya 1581, Lüneburg 1575, Pomerania 1569 ([§10.7.2](#s10-7-2)).

Senftenberg is typical of a small electoral town. **Senftenberg, *Kirchen-Ordnung für die Stadt
Senftenberg*, 1555** (Sehling 1, pp. 671–672):

<!-- doc 136 -->
> Alle sontage, hohe festa und feiertage sol den morgen fru hora 5 wie gewonlich metten mit dem
> invitatorio, psalmodia, lection des evangelii, teutsch respons. et benedicamus beschlossen
> werden. […] Es sol auch in der wochen auf die werkeltage alle tage den morgen umb 7 hora eine
> metten mit psalmodi, teutscher lection aus dem alten testament sampt dem benedictus collecten
> und benedicamus, nachmittage aber umb 2 hora eine vesper mit ihrer psalmodi, lection aus dem
> neuen testa

All Sundays, high feasts and holy days, in the morning early at the fifth hour, Matins shall be
held as is customary, with the invitatory, psalmody, the lesson of the Gospel, a German
responsory, and concluded with the *Benedicamus*. […] Also in the week on the working days,
every day in the morning about the seventh hour, [there shall be] a Matins with psalmody, a
German lesson out of the Old Testament, together with the *Benedictus*, collects and
*Benedicamus*; and in the afternoon about the second hour a Vespers with its psalmody, a lesson
out of the New Testa[ment] […]

#### <a id="s10-5-3"></a>10.5.3 Decline and transfer

**Moved from the Latin school to the German school.** By 1580 the Saxon visitors thought the
daily office kept the Latin scholars from their studies. In the great towns, on days without a
sermon, it was handed to the **German school** and reduced to a psalm, a chapter and a collect.
**Saxony, *Ordnung* of Duke August, 1580** (Sehling 1, p. 370):

<!-- doc 44 -->
> Wo auch in grossen stedten gebreuchlich, das man teglich metten und vesper auf die tage, da
> man nicht prediget, zuhalten pfleget, dardurch die schüler in der lateinischen schulen an
> ihrem studiren nicht wenig verseumet werden, soll hinfort, soviel das gesang belanget,
> dasselbige durch die deutschen schulen versehen, und allezeit ein psalm vor und einer nach
> gesungen, darzwischen aber ein capitel aus der bibel, sampt dem summario durch den diaconum
> gelesen, und mit den gewönlichen collecten beschlossen werden.

Where also in great towns it is the custom to keep Matins and Vespers daily on the days when
there is no preaching, whereby the scholars in the Latin schools are not a little hindered in
their studies, it shall henceforth, so far as the singing is concerned, be provided by the
German schools; and always a psalm shall be sung before and one after, but between them a
chapter out of the Bible, together with the summary, read by the deacon, and concluded with the
customary collects.

**The little hours fall away.** At Feuchtwangen in 1563 the chapter still sang Matins and Lauds
daily, but Prime, Terce, Sext and None had lapsed for some years. They clashed with the parish
sermon nearby, there were no scholars to sing, and "many spoke mockingly" of them. By then the
four little hours were sung in rotation, one a day. **Brandenburg-Ansbach-Kulmbach,
Feuchtwangen, 1563** (Sehling 11, p. 402):

<!-- doc 293 -->
> und der communicanten, die in stift gehörig, wenig, darzue bis anher von solchem singen und
> lesen von vilen schimpflich geredet und gehalten worden, sein solche horae und communion der
> ursachen halben und nit aus faul- oder treghait etzliche jar her underlassen und nicht
> gehalten worden.

and the communicants that belong to the chapter [being] few, and moreover, many having hitherto
spoken and held mockingly of such singing and reading, such hours and communion have for these
causes, and not out of sloth or idleness, for some years been left off and not kept.

**Other signs.**
- **Torgau 1529**: the schoolmasters complained that at seven they had to sing "private hours"
  in the church while the school waited. The visitors gave the hours to the altarists, though
  the masters were to keep the stipend and help when they could (Sehling 1, p. 677).
- **The Schönburg lordships**: the "hour-priests" of the castle are to sing the hours daily
  "slowly and distinctly", though the reformer "would rather advise" one or two sermons in the
  castle "instead of such hours, since no one or very few are bettered by them". The Matins he
  then gives begins with "*Deus in adjutorium* in Latin" and has "*Venite*, 4 psalms in German"
  (Sehling 2, p. 170).
- **Mülhausen 1524** (Reformed): Sehling's introduction notes that the council left the singing
  of Matins, Terce and Sext to the chaplains' discretion but kept None and Vespers
  (Sehling 20/2, p. 163).

---

### <a id="s10-6"></a>10.6 Who prayed the offices, and under what obligation

#### <a id="s10-6-1"></a>10.6.1 The schoolboys

**The office as school exercise.** In the parishes the office belonged to the Latin school. The
cantor led the boys in the choir, and the boys read the lessons. The orders give two reasons,
practice in the Bible and practice in public speaking. **Prussia, *Kirchenordnung und
Ceremonien*, 1568** (Sehling 4, p. 75):

<!-- doc 1833 -->
> Darauf soll ein knabe aus der bibel latine in usitato tono eine lectionem lesen, also lectio
> Jesaiae etc. prophetae, capite etc., und soll darauf, was solcher knabe latine gelesen, ein
> anderer deutsch lesen fur dem chor schlecht sine tono. Solche lectiones dienen dazu, dass die
> liebe jugend ein wenig den text der bibel fasse, denn es ja so gering nimmermehr abgehet, die
> liebe kinder behalten etwas davon. So ist es ihnen auch darzu nütze, das sie lernen und
> gewohnen in der kirchen nach ihrem berufe fur dem volke zu reden, und dasjenige, worzu sie
> erfordert werden, one furcht auszurichten.

Thereupon shall a boy read a lesson out of the Bible in Latin in the customary tone, thus:
"Lectio Isaiae prophetae, capite" etc.; and thereupon what the boy hath read in Latin shall
another read in German before the choir, plainly, without tone. Such lessons serve thereto, that
the dear youth may grasp a little of the text of the Bible; for it never goeth off so slightly
but the dear children retain something of it. So is it also profitable to them that they learn
and grow used to speak in the church before the people, according to their calling, and to
perform without fear that whereunto they are required.

The school's burden was weighed against its studies:
- At Wittenberg in 1533, if the boys had sung the Mass in the morning, "they shall sing no
  Vespers that day, that they be not too much hindered in their studies" (Sehling 1, p. 705).
- Saxony 1580 moved the weekday office from the Latin to the German school for the same reason
  ([§10.5.3](#s10-5-3)).

#### <a id="s10-6-2"></a>10.6.2 Canons, vicars and altarists: an obligation tied to the benefice

**Hours instead of Masses.** Where the endowed Masses fell away but the incomes remained, the
orders turned the holders of benefices into a choir for the hours. At Stendal in 1540 the vicars
keep their incomes on condition that they sing the hours daily and hear the sermons and theology
lectures. **Stendal, *Verordnung für die übrigen Kirchen*, 1540** (Sehling 3, p. 310):

<!-- doc 1784 -->
> Weil denn die privatmessen, darauf die vicarien instituirt gewesen, des offnen erkannten
> missbrauchs halben abgangen und dennoch den vicarien ihre einkommen davon bleiben, sollen sie
> hinfort, jede in ihren pfarrkirchen, täglich horas canonicas de tempore singen und in die
> predigt mit fleiss gehen, desgleichen auch die lectiones in theologia, die der superintendent
> allhier thun wird, visitiren. Dagegen sollen sie alle horas und memorien, die sie zuvor
> gesungen und gehalten, gänzlich fallen lassen.

Since now the private Masses, to which the vicars were instituted, have ceased by reason of
their open and acknowledged abuse, and yet their incomes from them remain to the vicars, they
shall henceforth, each in their parish churches, sing the canonical hours *de tempore* daily,
and go diligently to the sermon, and likewise attend the lectures in theology which the
superintendent here shall give. On the other hand they shall let fall altogether all hours and
memorials which they formerly sang and kept.

The Brandenburg town orders enforce this obligation with the loss of the benefice:
- **Cölln on the Spree, 1540**: every priest holding a benefice in the two churches is to sing
  the canonical hours *de tempore* daily in St Nicholas; "whatever priest refuseth this shall be
  deprived of his fief" (Sehling 3, p. 156).
- **Salzwedel, 1541**: all vicars and commendists resident in the town are to sing the hours
  daily "every morning, winter and summer, at six o'clock", on pain of losing the vicarage
  (Sehling 3, p. 267).

**Bonnus at Quakenbrück, 1543.** Hermann Bonnus gives two reasons for keeping the daily office
in the collegiate churches: the holders of prebends, "that they live not wholly in idleness",
and the scholars. **Stift Osnabrück, *Ordinatio Magistri Hermanni Bonni*, 1543**
(Sehling 7/1, p. 229):

<!-- doc 2097 -->
> Utile et necessarium in primis est, retinere in collegiatis ecclesiis exercitium sacrae
> scripturae et psalmorum: idque propter personas religiosas, quae possident praebendas et
> beneficia ecclesiastica, ne prorsus in otio vivant, deinde etiam propter scholasticos, quos
> plurimum conducit exercere diligenter in legendis et cantandis psalmis et lectionibus sacris
> quotidie.

It is above all useful and needful to retain in the collegiate churches the exercise of holy
Scripture and of the psalms: and that for the sake of the religious persons who possess prebends
and ecclesiastical benefices, that they live not wholly in idleness; and then also for the sake
of the scholars, whom it greatly profiteth to be diligently exercised daily in reading and
singing the psalms and the holy lessons.

#### <a id="s10-6-3"></a>10.6.3 The convents and their pastors

**Daily office with the pastor.** In the evangelical convents the pastor often led the office.
At the Cistercian convent of Leeden in Tecklenburg (1585) the conventuals and the abbess are to
meet "with their pastor every day in the morning at seven o'clock in the convent church". There
they say the morning prayer, sing a psalm, and hear a chapter of the Bible read and briefly
expounded by the pastor (Sehling 22, p. 247). At Keppel (1570) the preacher is to teach the nuns
the melodies of the German psalms ([§10.9.2](#s10-9-2)).

#### <a id="s10-6-4"></a>10.6.4 The congregation

**Sunday and feast-day offices for all.** Luther meant the weekday office for "the smaller
crowd" and the Sunday Mass and Vespers for "the whole congregation" ([§10.3.1](#s10-3-1)). The orders follow
this:
- Saturday and Sunday Vespers, Sunday Matins and festal Matins are public services, with sermon
  or catechism.
- On weekdays the offices are attended by whoever comes. At Naumburg the people sing a psalm
  with the scholars, "one verse after the other" (Sehling 2, p. 596).
- Saturday Vespers is also the hour of confession for those who will communicate. Kurland 1570
  explains Saturday Vespers as the time when servants and labourers are let off work "to prepare
  and make themselves ready" (Sehling 5, p. 83).

**Village Vespers in German.** In the villages there was no Latin school, and the orders give a
German Vespers led by the pastor and the sexton. **Lippe, *Kirchenordnung*, 1571**
(Sehling 21, p. 395):

<!-- doc 1462 -->
> Erstlich soll die Vesper umb zween schlegen alle Son- und Festabendt angefangen werden. Und
> sol der Pfarrherr neben seinem Küster und den Knaben, so der Custos zu leren bey sich hat, und
> jetzt auff den Dörffern gewöntlich, einen teutschen Psalm singen, Drauff den Hymnum nach
> gelegenheit der Sontage und Feste, Darnach den Lobgesang der Jungfrawen Marien und die
> Collecten oder Gebett neben dem Benedicamus. Es sol aber alles Teutsch auff den Dörffern
> gesungen werden, damit die einfeltige, ungeschickte Schüler der Küster und Beichtkinder auff
> dem Lande der Gottseligen Psalmen gewohnen […].

First, Vespers shall be begun at two o'clock on every Sunday and feast eve. And the pastor,
together with his sexton and the boys whom the sexton hath with him to teach (as is now
customary in the villages), shall sing a German psalm; thereupon the hymn according to the
occasion of the Sundays and feasts; thereafter the Song of the Virgin Mary, and the collect or
prayer, with the *Benedicamus*. But all shall be sung in German in the villages, that the
simple, unskilled scholars of the sexton and the penitents in the country may grow used to the
godly psalms […].

Other village provisions:
- **Prussia 1568**: "in small parishes and villages", one or two German psalms and a short
  catechism instruction at Vespers (Sehling 4, p. 75).
- **Lippe 1571 and Oldenburg 1573**: since there can be no Matins in the villages in winter, the
  pastors are to gather the people early in the morning in summer, from Easter to Michaelmas
  (Sehling 21, p. 396; 7/2.1, p. 1111).
- **Schwäbisch Hall 1543**: village Vespers "with a short sermon and psalms" is left to each
  pastor's discretion (Sehling 17/1, p. 170).

#### <a id="s10-6-5"></a>10.6.5 The pastors

**No breviary obligation.** No Lutheran order in the corpus binds a pastor to recite the hours
privately. The *Unterricht* of 1528 treats "praying the seven hours" as a human ordinance that
binds no conscience ([§10.3.4](#s10-3-4)).

**An exhortation instead.** The Merseburg synodal decree of 1544 noticed the result. Some
pastors, "now that they are discharged of the burden of the canonical hours, think they need
neither pray nor read any more". It answers with an exhortation, not a rule: daily prayer and
use of the psalter. **Merseburg, synodal decree, 1544** (Sehling 2, p. 13):

<!-- doc 1211 -->
> und dieweil sie nun der burde der horarum canonicarum entlediget, meinen, sie dürfen furder
> wider beten noch lesen, gehen die ganze woche mussig, ader warten der narung […]. Darumb
> sollen die pfarher ernstlich zum vleissigen teglichen gebet erinnert sein, dan so sie solches
> vorseumen, werden sie dem teufel raum lassen, und gottes und der obrickeit straf nicht
> empflihen. In sonderheit aber wollen sie sich im heiligen psalter vleissig uben, und den so
> vorechtlichen nicht liegen lassen.

and since they are now discharged of the burden of the canonical hours, they think they need
from henceforth neither pray nor read; they go idle the whole week, or wait upon their
livelihood […]. Therefore the pastors shall be earnestly admonished to diligent daily prayer;
for if they neglect the same, they will give place to the devil, and not escape the punishment
of God and of the magistrate. But especially let them exercise themselves diligently in the holy
psalter, and not let it lie so despised.

**The pastor's public duty.** What the orders do impose on pastors is the **public** office:
- **Pfalz-Neuburg 1576**: Saturday and feast-eve Vespers must be held in towns, markets and
  villages. "In case that no one at all came into the church", the pastor shall still have the
  bell rung and read a chapter of the Bible with its summary (Sehling 13, p. 178). The order
  adds that this keeps him at home on Saturday evening, preparing his sermon.
- **Saxony 1580**: the deacons and preachers are to be present at "the daily early prayer"
  (*teglichen frügebet*) as well as the sermons (Sehling 1, p. 422).
- **Hohenlohe 1588**: in time of war the countess ordered a daily prayer service (*das
  alltägliche Gebet*) in every parish, and the pastors were to urge their people to attend
  (Sehling 15, pp. 538–550).

#### <a id="s10-6-6"></a>10.6.6 Students and future pastors

**The Württemberg cloister schools, 1559.** The Great Church Order of Württemberg turned the
monasteries into schools for future ministers. Their day begins at four or five with *preces*: a
psalm read in course by one of the students, and a Latin prayer for the Church, the emperor, the
duke, the prelate and their studies. **Württemberg, *Ordnung der Klosterschulen*, 1559**
(Sehling 16, pp. 365–366):

<!-- doc 683 -->
> das alle Tag, es seien Feyer- oder Wercktag, vor Mittag, morgendts im Winter umb fünffe, im
> Sommer aber nach vier Uhrn, ungefahrlich, so sie durch des Klosters geleutte Glocken
> auffgemundert, Preces samentlich gehalten, und einer auß den Studiosen mit erhebter Stimm
> verstentlich einen Psalmen ex ordine, wie es die Ordnung geben würdt, lese. […] Hernach an
> einem jettlichen Wercktag alle Morgen, zu Sommers zeitten nach acht, Wintters zeit umb neun
> Uhr […], zween oder drey Psalmos, nach dem sie lang oder kurtz seind, mit den gewonlichen
> Christlichen Antiphonen de Tempore singen und darauff ein gantz Capitel auß dem alten
> Testament von anfang der Bibel nach seiner Ordnung verlesen und dasselbig mit dem Benedictus
> oder Symbolo Athanasii, alternis ein tag umb den andern, auch gewonlichen Christlichen
> Antiphonen de Tempore und Collect beschliessen.

that every day, be it holy day or working day, before noon, in the morning in winter at five,
but in summer after four o'clock or thereabouts, when they are roused by the convent's ringing
bells, they hold *preces* together, and one of the students read with raised voice, distinctly,
a psalm in order, as the order shall give it. […] Thereafter on every working day, every
morning, in summer after eight, in winter at nine o'clock […], [they shall] sing two or three
psalms, according as they be long or short, with the customary Christian antiphons *de tempore*,
and thereupon read a whole chapter out of the Old Testament in its order from the beginning of
the Bible, and conclude the same with the *Benedictus* or the Athanasian Creed, alternately one
day after the other, also with the customary Christian antiphons *de tempore* and a collect.

In the afternoon a chapter of the New Testament is read, with the *Magnificat* or the *Nunc
dimittis* alternately (Sehling 16, p. 366). One student is appointed each week as
*hebdomadarius* for the *preces* and another for the lessons (Sehling 16, p. 367).

**The Tübingen Stipendium, 1559.** The ducal stipendiaries at Tübingen, the theology students
who were to become Württemberg's pastors, are bound by their statutes to pray "every day,
morning and evening", reciting the psalms "one or two at a time until they are finished" and
then a set prayer (Sehling 17/1, p. 562). The medieval obligation of the clergy to the psalter
survives here as a rule of the seminary.

---

### <a id="s10-7"></a>10.7 The shape of the reformed offices

#### <a id="s10-7-1"></a>10.7.1 What was kept, cut and added

**The orders set out the liturgy.** Many orders give the office in detail, hour by hour:
Wittenberg 1525, Braunschweig 1528, Ansbach 1533, Goslar 1534, Pomerania 1535, Spandau 1541,
Bonnus 1543, Württemberg 1559, Keppel 1570, Lüneburg 1574. Their common features are these.

**Kept:**
- the **psalms** with their **antiphons**, sung in two choirs "verse by verse";
- the **lessons**, with **responsories** after them at Matins;
- the **office hymns**, if "pure";
- the **gospel canticles**: *Benedictus* at the morning office, *Magnificat* at Vespers, *Nunc
  dimittis* at Compline;
- the ***Te Deum*** at Sunday and festal Matins;
- the **Athanasian Creed** at Sunday Prime (Ansbach 1533, Goslar 1534, Pomerania 1535);
- the **Kyrie**, **Our Father**, the versicle *Ostende nobis*, the **collect** *de tempore* and
  the ***Benedicamus***;
- the **invitatory** and *Venite* at Matins (Senftenberg 1555, Frankenberg 1542, Keppel 1570).

**Cut:**
- everything *de sanctis* that asks for the saints' intercession, with the suffrages and the
  Marian antiphons;
- the **homilies and legends** at Matins, replaced by Scripture;
- the **preces**, which are dropped (Wittenberg 1525, Ansbach 1533) or replaced by the Litany
  (Altenburg 1533), though a short form survived ([§10.7.5](#s10-7-5));
- the blessings before the lessons, ***Jube, domne, benedicere*** and ***Tu autem, Domine***
  (Braunschweig 1528, Pomerania 1535, Frankenberg 1542);
- in Bugenhagen's orders, even the opening ***Deus in adiutorium*** and ***Domine, labia mea***
  (Wittenberg 1525, Pomerania 1535, Bonnus 1543). Bugenhagen explains in a note added in the
  Danish version. He does not forbid the words ("who would forbid it?"), but they are prayed
  "against the persecutors of the Church", and those are now the very men "who say *Deus in
  adiutorium* so many times a day" (Sehling 4, p. 350, n. 1);
- the **Office of the Dead** and vigils (Pomerania 1535).

**Shortened:**
- **three psalms** for Matins and three for Vespers (Luther 1523; Bugenhagen; Spandau 1541);
- **one nocturn** instead of three (Altenburg 1533; Lüneburg 1574);
- the little hours run together (Naumburg: Prime with Terce, Sext with None) or **rotated** one
  a day (Feuchtwangen 1563);
- Vespers and Compline **joined**, with Compline reduced to *Qui habitat* and the *Nunc
  dimittis* read without tone (Wittenberg 1525, Pomerania 1535, Braunschweig 1528).

**Added:**
- the **psalter in course**, sung through in order from day to day rather than by the old weekly
  distribution: monthly at Feuchtwangen 1563 and in the Mecklenburg convents 1572;
- the **Bible in course** (*lectio continua*): Old Testament at Matins, New Testament at
  Vespers, or the reverse, read through "twice or more in a year" (Pomerania 1535), "in one or
  two years" (Ansbach 1533), or "the Old Testament once and the New Testament three times a
  year" (Mecklenburg 1572);
- a **German lesson** after the Latin one, or a German chapter with Veit Dietrich's
  **summaries** (Naumburg, Saxony 1580, Keppel 1570);
- **German hymns** and the German Litany, especially in the convents and village offices;
- in the evangelical towns, a **sermon** or **catechism** joined to Vespers.

#### <a id="s10-7-2"></a>10.7.2 Bible lessons in place of homilies

**Pfalz-Neuburg 1543** gives the clearest rule for the Matins lessons. Where nine lessons are
kept, three come from the historical books, three from the prophets, and the last three from the
Epistles and the Gospel. Each day continues where the last left off. **Pfalz-Neuburg,
*Kirchenordnung*, 1543** (Sehling 13, pp. 77–78):

<!-- doc 386 -->
> doch mit der maß, das man zur metten nicht homilias lese, sonder lectiones aus der biblia. Die
> mögen in den stiften und clöstern, da man teglich metten singt, also geordnet werden, das,
> wann man novem lectiones helt, drei aus den historischen büchern der bibel als Mose, Josua,
> Judicum, Ruth, Samuel, der Könige und Chronica, […] darnach drei aus den propheten und der
> letsten dreier die ersten zwo aus den episteln, die dritte und letsten aber aus dem evangelio
> gelesen werden. […] und sollen also aufeinander gehn, daß, wo man heut aufhöret, da sol man
> morgen wider anheben und also die heiligen schrift ordenlich nacheinander lesen, alweg ein
> zimlich lange lection, wie bis anher der brauch gewest ist.

yet with this measure, that at Matins no homilies be read, but lessons out of the Bible. These
may be so ordered in the chapters and convents where Matins is sung daily, that when nine
lessons are kept, three be read from the historical books of the Bible, as Moses, Joshua,
Judges, Ruth, Samuel, the Kings and Chronicles, […] thereafter three from the prophets, and of
the last three, the first two from the Epistles, but the third and last from the Gospel. […] And
they shall so follow upon one another, that where one leaveth off today, there one shall begin
again tomorrow, and so read the holy Scripture orderly one after another, always a fairly long
lesson, as hath been the custom hitherto.

The chapters of Prime, Terce, Sext, None and Compline are likewise to be read in course from the
Bible, "so that where one leaveth off at Prime, there one shall begin again at Terce"
(Sehling 13, p. 78).

#### <a id="s10-7-3"></a>10.7.3 A complete morning office: Braunschweig, 1528

**The school Matins.** Bugenhagen's Braunschweig order describes the boys' daily morning office
in full. Two boys intone an antiphon and a Matins psalm, and the choirs sing it with one or two
more and an octonary of Psalm 119, which is the psalm of the old little hours. Three boys read
the Latin lesson in the Matins tone, and a fourth reads it in German. Then follow the
*Benedictus* and the closing prayers (Sehling 6/1, pp. 400–401). **Braunschweig,
*Kirchenordnung*, 1528** (Sehling 6/1, p. 401):

<!-- doc 1983 -->
> Balde darup schal de cantor alleyne singen dat erste halve versch vamme Benedictus nach deme
> tono der antiphen, de he gedenket, nach deme Benedictus to singen. Dat Benedictus schal
> geendet werden na gewänheit up beiden chören. Na der antiphen late me de kyndere up de kne
> vallen unde segge: Kyrie eleison, Christe eleison, Kyrie eleison; Pater noster. De predicante
> spreke: Et ne nos. Ostende nobis, Domine, misericordiam tuam. Responsio: Et salutare tuum da
> nobis. Dominus vobiscum. Oremus cum collecta. Rursum: Dominus vobiscum. Darup singen twe
> kyndere Benedicamus. Dit alle, weme id gewanen wert, wert kume eyne halve stunde waren.

Straightway thereupon shall the cantor alone sing the first half verse of the *Benedictus*, in
the tone of the antiphon which he thinketh to sing after the *Benedictus*. The *Benedictus*
shall be finished, as is customary, in both choirs. After the antiphon let the children fall on
their knees, and say: *Kyrie eleison, Christe eleison, Kyrie eleison; Pater noster*. The
preacher shall say: *Et ne nos*. *Ostende nobis, Domine, misericordiam tuam*. Response: *Et
salutare tuum da nobis*. *Dominus vobiscum*. *Oremus*, with the collect. Again: *Dominus
vobiscum*. Thereupon two children sing the *Benedicamus*. All this, when one is used to it, will
scarcely last half an hour.

**The evening office.** The evening office is built the same way. It has the Vesper psalms, four
Old Testament lessons, a ferial hymn ("the precious *hymni feriales*, every day one, or at times
other fine hymns of Ambrose, Prudentius etc."), and the *Magnificat*. On feast eves and feasts
the *Nunc dimittis* is added after the *Benedicamus*, "read slowly … without tone", followed by
the Compline hymn *Jesu redemptor saeculi* (Sehling 6/1, p. 401). Matins, Lauds, the little
hours, Vespers and Compline are all present in miniature, folded into two half-hour services.

#### <a id="s10-7-4"></a>10.7.4 Sunday Vespers in a Lutheran town, 1581

By the later century the town Vespers was a preaching service built on the old frame. **Hoya,
*Kirchenordnung*, 1581** (Sehling 6/2, p. 1150):

<!-- doc 2065 -->
> Deß Sontags sol man umb ein uhr zur vesper leuten, und sol der schulmeister mit den knaben in
> den chor gehen und drey psalm Davids mit einer antiphen singen. Darauf sol ein knabe eine
> lateinische lection aus dem neuen testament und folgends ein ander knabe deudsch darauf lesen.
> Darnach sol der organist den hymnum schlagen. Nach dem hymno singet man einen deudschen psalm.
> Darauf folget die predigt. Nach der predigt singet man abermal einen deudschen psalm, darauf
> das Magnificat. Nach dem Magnificat die collect und das Benedicamus.

On Sunday one shall ring to Vespers at one o'clock, and the schoolmaster shall go with the boys
into the choir and sing three psalms of David with an antiphon. Thereupon shall a boy read a
Latin lesson out of the New Testament, and next another boy [read] it in German. Thereafter the
organist shall play the hymn. After the hymn a German psalm is sung. Thereupon followeth the
sermon. After the sermon a German psalm is sung again, thereupon the *Magnificat*. After the
*Magnificat* the collect and the *Benedicamus*.

#### <a id="s10-7-5"></a>10.7.5 The *preces*, the suffrages and the Litany

**What the old office had.** Three kinds of intercession closed the medieval hours. The *preces*
were a chain of Kyrie, Our Father, Creed and versicles said kneeling on ferias, chiefly at
Lauds, Prime, Vespers and Compline. The editor of the Ansbach order glosses them as
"intercessions (as in the Litany), inserted in a set, changing manner into the several orders of
prayer" (Sehling 11, p. 313, n. 10). The *suffragia* were commemorations with antiphon, versicle
and collect, chiefly of the saints, added after the collect of the day. The **Litany** of the
Saints belonged to Rogation and to particular days. The orders treat the three differently: the
full *preces* were cut, a short form was kept, the saints' suffrages were dropped, and the
Litany came in, in Luther's corrected Latin and his German, as the new common intercession.

**The full preces cut.** Wittenberg's castle church dropped them in 1525. **Wittenberg, *Wie es
einer zeit mit den ceremonien der kirchen gehalten wirt*, 1525** (Sehling 1, p. 699):

<!-- doc 147 -->
> Ad primam vero legatur collecta vulgaris, preces (quas vocant) ubique omnino omittantur.

But at Prime let the common collect be read; the *preces* (as they call them) shall be wholly
left out everywhere.

The Ansbach chapters were told the same in 1533, and in the same breath given the Litany and two
suffrages. **Brandenburg-Ansbach-Kulmbach, *Ordnung singens und lesens bei den Stiften*, 1533**
(Sehling 11, pp. 313–314):

<!-- doc 276 -->
> Die preces sollen sie alle tag underlassen. […] Uns sehe auch fur gut an, das sie am
> wenigstens ain mal in der wochen als am freitag die letanei hielten, dieweil sant Paulus
> vermanet, man soll fur alle stend bitten, 1.Tim.2, [1f.], damit das gemain gebet auch in der
> kirchen plib. Alle suffragia de sanctis sollen sie underlassen; dann sie stellen das vertrauen
> in die hailigen wider das erst gebot Gottes. Allein mogen sie an den werktagen suffragia pro
> pace und pro peccatis halten.

The *preces* they shall leave off every day. […] It seemeth good to us also that at the least
once in the week, as on Friday, they hold the Litany, since Saint Paul exhorteth that one should
pray for all estates, 1 Timothy 2, that the common prayer may abide in the church also. All
suffrages *de sanctis* they shall leave off, for they set trust in the saints, against the first
commandment of God. Only on the working days they may hold the suffrages *pro pace* and *pro
peccatis*.

**The short preces kept.** What survived in the Bugenhagen orders was the core of the old ferial
*preces*, said kneeling after the gospel canticle: *Kyrie*, Our Father, *Et ne nos*, the
versicle *Ostende nobis*, *Dominus vobiscum*, the collect and *Benedicamus*. Braunschweig 1528
is quoted above ([§10.7.3](#s10-7-3)). The same chain stands in Wittenberg 1525 after the *Magnificat*
(Sehling 1, p. 698), Hamburg 1529 (Sehling 5, p. 523), Lübeck 1531 (Sehling 5, p. 348), the
Pomeranian *Pia ordinatio* of 1535 after the *Benedictus* (Sehling 4, p. 349), Goslar 1534
(Sehling 7/2.2, pp. 263–264), Frankenberg 1542 (Sehling 7/2.2, p. 277), Schleswig-Holstein 1542
(Sehling 23, p. 142), Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel 1543 (Sehling 6/1, p. 50) and Hildesheim 1544
(Sehling 7/2.1, p. 849). In the parish orders the children kneel and a preacher or one of the
boys says the versicle.

**A full German preces: the Mecklenburg convents.** The Mecklenburg convent order of 1572 kept a
complete set of *preces* in German after the *Benedictus* every day: Kyrie, Creed, Our Father,
and a chain of versicles for mercy, the magistrates, the clergy, the people and peace, ending in
three collects. **Mecklenburg, *Klosterordnung*, 1572** (Sehling 5, pp. 258–259):

<!-- doc 1926 -->
> Hierauf folgen diese gebete durch das ganze jahr: Kyrie eleison, Christe eleison, Kyrie
> eleison. oder Herre erbarme dich, Christe erbarme dich, Herre erbarme dich. Darnach spricht
> die jungfrau, so das gebet angefangen, mit lauter stimme die bekäntniss des christlichen
> glaubens: Ich glaube in gott vater etc. und das Vater unser etc. Der chor antwortet: Sondern
> erlöse uns von dem bösen. Die jungfrau: Herr erzeige uns deine gnad Der chor: Und beweise uns
> deine hülfe. Die jungfrau: Herr hilf unser obrigkeit Der chor: Und höre uns, wen wir dich
> anrufen. Die jungfrau : Deine priester wollest mit gerechtigkeit kleiden Der chor: Und deine
> heiligen sollen frölig sein. Die jungfrau: Hilf deinem volke, herr Jesu Christ, Der chor: Und
> segne, was dein erbtheil ist. Die jungfrau: Verleihe uns frieden gnediglich, Herr gott zu
> unsern zeiten. Der chor: Den es ist kein ander nicht, Der für uns könnte streiten, Den du,
> unser gott, alleine. Die jungfrau: Schaff in uns gott ein rein herze. Der chor: Und nim deinen
> heiligen geist nicht von uns. Die jungfrau : Der herr sei mit euch Der chor: Und mit deinem
> geist. Lasset uns beten: Hierauf folgen täglich drei collecten: Die erste von der zeit, Die
> andere vom frieden. […] Die dritte für gottes wort und erhaltung in wahren glauben.

Hereupon follow these prayers through the whole year: *Kyrie eleison, Christe eleison, Kyrie
eleison*; or, Lord, have mercy; Christ, have mercy; Lord, have mercy. Thereafter the virgin who
began the prayer saith with a loud voice the confession of the Christian faith, I believe in God
the Father etc., and the Our Father etc. The choir answereth: But deliver us from evil. The
virgin: Lord, show us thy grace. The choir: And show us thy help. The virgin: Lord, help our
magistrates. The choir: And hear us when we call upon thee. The virgin: Thy priests wilt thou
clothe with righteousness. The choir: And thy saints shall be joyful. The virgin: Help thy
people, Lord Jesus Christ. The choir: And bless that which is thine inheritance. The virgin:
Grant us peace graciously, Lord God, in our days. The choir: For there is none other that could
fight for us, but thou, our God, alone. The virgin: Create in us, God, a clean heart. The choir:
And take not thy Holy Spirit from us. The virgin: The Lord be with you. The choir: And with thy
spirit. Let us pray. Hereupon follow daily three collects: the first of the season, the other
for peace, […] the third for God's word and preservation in the true faith.

The versicles are the old *preces* of Lauds and Vespers in German: *Ostende nobis*, *Domine
salvum fac regem*, *Sacerdotes tui induantur iustitia*, *Salvum fac populum tuum*, *Da pacem*
and *Cor mundum*, with Luther's "Verleih uns Frieden" in place of *Fiat pax*. At Vespers the
same order sets the Kyrie, Creed, Ten Commandments and Our Father before "*Ostende nobis domine
misericordiam tuam* […] *Domine salvum fac regem* […] together with the other suffrages, in
German (or in Latin, if the virgins understand it), as they are set down above at Matins"
(Sehling 5, p. 259).

**The saints' suffrages dropped.** The Saxon visitors of 1529 close Vespers "with the customary
versicles and collects, the suffrages of the saints excepted". **Belzig, *Ordnung der Stadt
Belzig*, 1529** (Sehling 1, p. 527):

<!-- doc 63 -->
> darnach aber das magnificat mit den gewonlichen versikeln und collecten, suffragia sanctorum
> ausgenomen, und durch die kirchen etwan geistlich lied gesungen werden.

but thereafter the *Magnificat* with the customary versicles and collects, the *suffragia
sanctorum* excepted, and some spiritual song be sung by the church.

The same clause stands in the visitation orders for Eilenburg (Sehling 1, p. 560) and Niemegk
(Sehling 1, p. 616). Coburg 1545 ends Vespers with the collect of the season and *Benedicamus*,
"so that all suffrages be left out" (Sehling 1, p. 543). Bonnus's order for the Osnabrück
chapters (1543) puts the "*Suffragia et invocationes sanctorum*" with vigils and prayers for the
dead among things "contrary to the word of God" (Sehling 7/1, p. 229).

**Suffrages that stayed.** Only intercessions for the living stayed. Ansbach kept *pro pace* and
*pro peccatis* (above). The Transylvanian Saxons kept three suffrages, for the king, for the
remission of sins and for peace, with their versicles and collects, after the Creed in the
service that replaced the Mass when no one communed
(Sehling 24, p. 223; [Chapter 13](#ch13), [§13.22.1](#s13-22-1)).

The suffrage for peace survived most widely as the *Da pacem* in Latin and German, with a
collect *pro pace*, after the *Magnificat* (Dresden, Kreuzkirche 1574, Sehling 1, p. 555;
Pomerania 1542, Sehling 4, p. 354).

**The Litany at Vespers.** The Litany most often took the place of the *Magnificat* or followed
it, and the Saturday and feast-eve Vespers were its usual hour. Bugenhagen's Pomeranian order
has the boys read Luther's Latin Litany after the Saturday Vespers lessons, but not on the eve
of a feast. **Pomerania, *Kirchenordnung*, 1535** (Sehling 4, p. 340):

<!-- doc 1856 -->
> Balde up de lectiones schölen dree eder veere iungen, wo de scholmeisters will, de latinische
> letanie lesen ut dem sankbökeken doctoris Martini Luther. Unde dat chor schal stedes
> entwerden, wo im sankbökeken vorvatet is, dar up lest de predicant eine collect, pro ecclesia,
> unde na dem amen singe man benedicamus. Overst tor vesper, went idt des anderen dages
> sunderlick fest is, so schal me na den lectionibus nicht de letanie lesen, sundern dat
> magnificat latinisch singen mit einer antiphen

Straightway after the lessons shall three or four boys, as the schoolmasters will, read the
Latin Litany out of Doctor Martin Luther's little song-book; and the choir shall always answer,
as is set down in the song-book; thereupon the preacher readeth a collect *pro ecclesia*, and
after the Amen let *Benedicamus* be sung. But at Vespers, when the next day is a special feast,
one shall not read the Litany after the lessons, but sing the *Magnificat* in Latin with an
antiphon.

Once a week the boys sang the German Litany with the people before the sermon instead of the
office (Sehling 4, p. 342). The Pomeranian order of 1542 allows the Latin Litany in place of the
*Magnificat* "when one keepeth plainly *dominicaliter*, as in Advent and Lent, and otherwise
when one will", followed by the collect *pro ecclesia* and *Da pacem* (Sehling 4, p. 354). The
*Agenda* of 1569 makes it monthly. **Pomerania, *Agenda*, 1569** (Sehling 4, p. 435):

<!-- doc 1865 -->
> Alle maente schal men in der vesper am viravende singen, ein mal loco magnificat, dat düdische
> magnificat, mit siner antiphen, Christum unsen heiland etc., unde ein mal de latinische
> letanie, loco magnificat. Dar na lest de prester eine collecte düdisch edder latinisch, unde
> beslüt dat chor mit dem benedicamus, unde singet dar up, da pacem domine, flexis genibus,
> latinisch edder düdisch.

Every month one shall sing at Vespers on the eve [of the holy day], once *loco Magnificat*, the
German *Magnificat* with its antiphon, "Christum unsern Heiland" etc., and once the Latin Litany
*loco Magnificat*. Thereafter the priest readeth a collect in German or Latin, and the choir
closeth with the *Benedicamus*, and singeth thereupon *Da pacem, Domine*, on bended knees, in
Latin or German.

Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel puts the Latin Litany after the hymn at the Vespers of holy eves, sung
by two or three children, and leaves the German Litany for the weekday sermon. **Brunswick-
Wolfenbüttel, *Christlike kerken-ordeninge*, 1543** (Sehling 6/1, p. 51):

<!-- doc 1972 -->
> Na dem hymno scholen twe edder dre kindere balde de latinische litania singen. Darna eine
> collecten und Benedicamus. Overst de düdesche litania mach men in der weken einmal na der
> predike laten singen, dat de ganze kercke antwerde, wenn de parhere wil.

After the hymn shall two or three children straightway sing the Latin Litany; thereafter a
collect and *Benedicamus*. But the German Litany one may let be sung once in the week after the
sermon, that the whole church answer, if the parson will.

The Sunday and feast-day Vespers are to be held "without the litany" (Sehling 6/1, p. 53), and
Hildesheim 1544 copies the rule (Sehling 7/2.1, pp. 850–851). Other places:
- **Wittenberg 1533**: the Latin Litany in the choir after the sermon at Saturday Vespers,
  closed with a Latin versicle, collect and *Benedicamus* (Sehling 1, pp. 703, 705);
- **Bremen 1534**: the German Litany after the *Magnificat* at the daily evening office of the
  schools (Sehling 7/2.2, p. 458);
- **Osnabrück 1543**: the German or Latin Litany at times "in the morning, also at Vespers, for
  all needs of body and soul that lie upon us" (Sehling 7/1, p. 256);
- **Thorn 1575**: on Fridays, in place of Vespers, on alternate weeks a figured Passion, or a
  figured piece followed by the Latin Litany with a collect (Sehling 4, p. 239).

**The Litany at the morning office.** The Litany was also joined to the morning office:
- **Hamburg 1556**: after the *Benedictus* "at times the *Quicunque vult*, at times the Litany
  in Latin or German *cum oratione*" (Sehling 5, p. 553);
- **Danzig 1557**: on Friday the weekday Matins "with the litanies to be sung besides"
  (Sehling 4, p. 181);
- **Remse 1533** (with the Altenburg convent): the nuns hold the German Litany "every week on
  Wednesday and Friday after the *Benedictus*, before the collect" (Sehling 1, p. 652).

The Brandenburg convents sang it after Prime. **Crevese, *Visitations-Rezess* for the
Benedictine convent, 1541** (Sehling 3, p. 203):

<!-- doc 1762 -->
> Doch schollen die junkfrowen alle sondage, mondage, middewoke und fridage die litanei, wo in
> drudde deil der ordnung to finden mit aller andacht des morgens na der prime singen und alle
> dartho kommen.

Yet the virgins shall every Sunday, Monday, Wednesday and Friday sing the Litany, as it is to be
found in the third part of the order, with all devotion in the morning after Prime, and all
shall come thereto.

The visitors repeated the rule, for Monday, Wednesday and Friday, at Spandau in 1541
(Sehling 3, p. 305) and in the Salzwedel convent in 1579 (Sehling 3, p. 272).

**The Litany in place of the *preces* and the *Salve*.** At the Altenburg chapter in 1533 the
canons were to hold "for the *preces* the pure new Litany" ([§10.4.2](#s10-4-2)). At Heilbronn in 1532 the
evening *Salve* became "a blessing for sleep": the schoolmaster and his boys sing "a German song
of praise, as the Litany, or *Mitten wir im Leben sind*, or *Da pacem Domine*", with a collect
(Sehling 17/1, p. 302).

**What was not found.** No order keeps the Litany of the Saints with its invocations in any
office, and no order uses *suffragia* in the liturgy for anything but the saints' commemorations
or the three intercessions for peace, sins and the ruler. The Mass and the weekday prayer
services, where the Litany was most at home, are treated in
[Chapter 13](#ch13), [§13.22](#s13-22).

---

### <a id="s10-8"></a>10.8 Latin, German, or both

#### <a id="s10-8-1"></a>10.8.1 Latin: chapters, schools, and the towns

**Latin for the learned.** The full cursus in the chapters stayed Latin ([§10.4.2](#s10-4-2)):
- **Brandenburg 1540** "in Latin … according to each bishopric's Breviary";
- **Goslar 1534**, where Widensee "holds fast to the use of the Latin language"
  (Sehling 7/2.2, p. 199);
- **Naumburg cathedral**, with a German lesson added;
- the canons' orders of **Bugenhagen** and **Bonnus**.

**The schools.** The school offices were Latin by design. Luther wanted "to keep and exercise
the youth in the Latin tongue in the Bible" ([§10.3.3](#s10-3-3)). Wittenberg 1533 forbids German singing by
the boys except when the people sing with them. **Wittenberg, *Kirchen-Ordnung für die Stadt
Wittenberg*, 1533** (Sehling 1, p. 703):

<!-- doc 148 -->
> Der schulmeister soll mit den kindern nicht stets einerlei singen, sondern mancherlei
> antiphon, responsoria, hymnos und andere gesenge, so rein aus der heiligen schrift genomen
> sein. […] Distincte und verstendig soll man psalmen und lectiones lesen und nicht ungeschickt
> singen. Deutsch sollen die schüler nicht singen, on allein, wenn das volk mitsinget.

The schoolmaster shall not always sing one thing with the children, but divers antiphons,
responsories, hymns and other chants that are taken purely out of holy Scripture. […] Distinctly
and with understanding shall the psalms and lessons be read, and not sung unskilfully. In German
the scholars shall not sing, save only when the people sing with them.

**Understanding the Latin.** Where Latin stayed, the orders tried to make it understood:
- **Braunschweig 1528**: "better diligence shall be applied, that the children learn to
  understand the Latin which they sing and read" (Sehling 6/1, p. 400).
- **Lohr 1588**: the Latin Vesper psalms "shall be explained in the school as far as needful, so
  far as it is possible to grasp them" (Sehling 11, p. 699).

#### <a id="s10-8-2"></a>10.8.2 German: convents and villages

**German psalmody in the convents.** Pfalz-Neuburg 1543 wants the women of the convents to psalm
in German, on the old tones. **Pfalz-Neuburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1543** (Sehling 13, p. 78):

<!-- doc 386 -->
> Und dieweil die ganz biblia diser zeit fleißig verteutscht, zuvor aber der psalter dermaßen an
> tag gebracht, das er im teutschen liechter ist dann in andern sprachen, so sollen die frauen
> in den klöstern lernen teutsch psallirn in gewonlichem ton, wie sie lateinisch pflegen, und
> ire lectiones, capitula und collecten teutsch lesen, damit sie dester mer gebessert und zu
> reichlicher erkantnus Gottis worts mögen kommen.

And since the whole Bible hath at this time been diligently put into German, and the psalter
above all hath been so brought to light that it is clearer in German than in other tongues, the
women in the convents shall learn to psalm in German in the customary tone, as they are wont [to
do] in Latin, and read their lessons, chapters and collects in German, that they may be the more
edified and come to a richer knowledge of God's word.

**German instead of the hours.** Other convent orders replace the Latin hours with a German
office of psalms, a chapter and a canticle. **Kloster Remse, *Ein kurze christliche ordnung in
das junkfrau closter*, 1533** (Sehling 1, p. 652):

<!-- doc 125 -->
> so sollen sie hinfur an stat der metten, prim, terz, sext, non, lesen drei deutsche psalmen,
> ein capitel aus den evangelisten an Sant Mathes anzufahen, das benedictus und ein reine
> collecten von der zeit; fur die vesper desgleichen auch drei psalm, ein capitel aus Sant Pauls
> episteln, der zum Romern anzufahen, das magnificat und ein collecten alles deutsch.

they shall henceforth, in place of Matins, Prime, Terce, Sext [and] None, read three German
psalms, a chapter out of the evangelists beginning at St Matthew, the *Benedictus* and a pure
collect of the season; for Vespers likewise also three psalms, a chapter out of St Paul's
epistles, beginning at that to the Romans, the *Magnificat* and a collect, all in German.

**The seven hours in German.** The Nassau-Dillenburg order for the convent of **Keppel (1570)**
keeps all seven hours, Matins, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers and Compline, but in German. It
gives the reason that the old Church divided its spiritual exercises into set times "in
remembrance of the bitter passion and death of our Lord Jesus Christ". **Nassau-Dillenburg,
*Ordnung für das Kloster Keppel*, 1570** (Sehling 10, p. 133):

<!-- doc 181 -->
> wöllenn wir, das dieselbige auch noch also gehalltenn werden, doch inn teutscher, verstendiger
> sprache, ihnen selbst unnd andern zur besserung und erbawung. Unnd sollenn derohalbenn alle
> closterjungfrawen deß morgens zur mettenzeit, darnach zur prim, tertz, sext unnd non, gegen
> abendt aber zur vesperzeit unnd complet, mit zucht unnd andacht miteinander inn den chor
> gehenn unnd inn gemein zu allenn zeiten erstlich die antiphon: Kom, heyliger geist, mit einem
> deutschenn verß unnd collect de spiritu sancto singenn.

we will that the same be still so kept, yet in the German understandable tongue, to their own
and others' amendment and edification. And therefore all the convent virgins shall in the
morning at the time of Matins, thereafter at Prime, Terce, Sext and None, but toward evening at
the time of Vespers and Compline, go together into the choir with discipline and devotion, and
at all times first sing together the antiphon "Komm, Heiliger Geist", with a German verse and
the collect of the Holy Ghost.

The Matins that follows has a German *Venite*, three psalms in course "with a short summary
before or after each", a German hymn "in place of the antiphon", an Old Testament lesson with
Veit Dietrich's summary, and so on. On feasts the psalms and lessons are those "noted in their
Breviary" (Sehling 10, pp. 133–134). Sehling's introduction notes an earlier Nassau order of
1558 that "prescribed the keeping of the seven hours in the German language"
(Sehling 10, p. 31).

**The Mecklenburg convents, 1572.** The Mecklenburg convents read the whole psalter monthly and
the Bible yearly, "in understandable German mother tongue" (Sehling 5, p. 257). Their daily
office is led by the domina and the nuns in weekly turn. It opens with the German versicle "Herr
thue meine lippen uf" and its *Gloria Patri* (Sehling 5, p. 257).

**Villages.** In the villages the office was German: "all shall be sung in German in the
villages" (Lippe 1571, [§10.6.4](#s10-6-4)).

#### <a id="s10-8-3"></a>10.8.3 Both

**Mixed Latin and German.** Many orders mix the two languages within the same office.
- **The lessons.** Bugenhagen and his followers have the lesson read in Latin and then in German
  (Braunschweig 1528, Prussia 1568, Hoya 1581). Luther's *Deutsche Messe* had already done so
  ([§10.3.3](#s10-3-3)).
- **The parishes in Pfalz-Neuburg, 1543.** At Vespers "a whole German chapter out of the New
  Testament [is to be read] instead of the Latin, and concluded with a German collect". The same
  applies "in all the other hours that are sung in the parish churches", that "the lessons and
  chapters together with the collects be kept in the German tongue for the people's sake"
  (Sehling 13, p. 78).
- **The Lüneburg convents, 1574.** The convents mix Latin and German psalms in each hour.
  **Lüneburg, *Klosterordnung* of Duke Wilhelm the Younger, 1574** (Sehling 6/1, p. 620):

<!-- doc 2010 -->
> so sollen in der metten nicht mehr dan drei lateinische und ein teutscher psalmen und zwo
> lectiones, dero eine soll ein halb oder dritte teil von einem capittel im neuen testament
> teutsch sein, und die collect und was sonst mehr gewonlich und christlich ist, darbei zu
> singen, gesungen und gelesen werden. Wan aber sonst festtage sein, sollen sie vier lateinische
> und zwen teutsche psalmen und drey lectiones […] singen und lesen.

there shall be sung and read at Matins no more than three Latin and one German psalm, and two
lessons, whereof one shall be a half or a third part of a chapter of the New Testament in
German, and the collect and whatever else is customary and Christian to sing therewith. But when
there are feast days, they shall sing and read four Latin and two German psalms and three
lessons […].

Prime and Terce have "a Latin and a German psalm and a collect". Sext and None have "two Latin
and one German psalm and a collect". At Compline the hymn "Christe, der du bist Tag und Licht"
is sung "in German" (Sehling 6/1, p. 621). Matins is moved from midnight to four or five in the
morning, "since the choir virgins grow daily older and more infirm" (Sehling 6/1, p. 620).

---

### <a id="s10-9"></a>10.9 The music

#### <a id="s10-9-1"></a>10.9.1 The old chant kept

**"Out of the former choir books."** The chapters kept their medieval chant books. Brandenburg
1540 orders the office sung "according to each bishopric's Breviary, out of the former choir
books" ([§10.4.2](#s10-4-2)). Verden cathedral in 1606 still sings Vespers "as the old order bringeth with it"
(Sehling 7/1, p. 153). The convents kept their Breviaries, corrected (Spandau 1541; Lüneburg
1555, [§10.4.4](#s10-4-4)). The Keppel order of 1570 refers its nuns to "their Breviary" for the feasts.

**The old tones.** The orders also keep the old reciting tones:
- **Pfalz-Neuburg 1543**: even when the nuns psalm in German, they are to do it "in the
  customary tone, as they are wont in Latin" ([§10.8.2](#s10-8-2)).
- **Bugenhagen**: the lessons are sung "with such a tone as one is wont to read lessons at
  Matins", with the cadence of the old prophecy tone, "*sol sol sol la sol fa fa*"
  (Sehling 6/1, p. 400; Sehling 4, p. 349).
- **Wittenberg 1533**: the boys end each lesson "as one was wont to read or sing the prophecies,
  *sol sol mi fa sol sol*" (Sehling 1, p. 703; see [Chapter 4](#ch4),
  [§4.5.1](#s4-5-1)).
- **Prussia 1568**: the Latin lesson is read "*in usitato tono*", the German one "without tone"
  ([§10.6.1](#s10-6-1)).

#### <a id="s10-9-2"></a>10.9.2 The new chant books: Spangenberg and Lossius

**The Lutheran antiphoners.** From the 1540s the old office chant reached Lutheran schools and
churches in two printed Lutheran collections:
- Johann Spangenberg's *Cantiones ecclesiasticae latinae … Kirchengesenge Deudsch* (Magdeburg
  1545);
- Lucas Lossius's *Psalmodia, hoc est, cantica sacra veteris ecclesiae selecta* (Nürnberg 1553,
  with a preface by Melanchthon; second edition Wittenberg 1561).

Both preserved the medieval antiphons, responsories, hymns and psalm tones, purged of what was
*de sanctis*. Several orders require them by name. **Mecklenburg, *Conformitas ceremoniarum*, c.
1560** (Sehling 5, p. 288):

<!-- doc 1936 -->
> Es wird für gut angesehen und notig eracht, das man in allen kirchen halten sol Lucae Lossii
> psalmodia und sol sich das chor darnach richten.

It is deemed good and held necessary that Lucas Lossius's *Psalmodia* be kept in all churches,
and that the choir order itself thereafter.

**Oldenburg 1573** wants "a right, pure cantional" in every church and school: "that of the old
Master Johann Spangenberg or of Lucas Lossius, together with the German hymnbook of Dr Martin
Luther". The organist alternates with the choir in the responsory, hymn and *Magnificat*.
**Oldenburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1573** (Sehling 7/2.1, p. 1085):

<!-- doc 2149 -->
> Wo orgeln sind, sol nach den psalmen der organist ein moteten spielen, darauf die lectio
> gelesen wird, nach welcher der organist das responsorium oder hymnum sol anfahen
> fortzuschlahen, wie sich denn alwegen dergegen der schulmeister und organist miteinander
> vergleichen sollen, und alsdenn in dem Magnificat ein vers umb den andern schlagen und singen.
> Zu der behülf ist vonnöten, das in allen kirchen und schulen ein rechtes, reines cantional
> stetigs zur hand sey, als nemlich des alten herrn Johan. Spangebergii oder Lucae Lossii sampt
> dem deudschen gesangbuch D. Martini Lutheri.

Where there are organs, the organist shall play a motet after the psalms, whereupon the lesson
is read; after which the organist shall begin to play the responsory or hymn, as the
schoolmaster and organist shall always agree with one another thereon; and then in the
*Magnificat* play and sing one verse after the other. To this end it is needful that in all
churches and schools a right, pure cantional be always at hand, namely that of the old Master
Johann Spangenberg or of Lucas Lossius, together with the German hymnbook of Dr Martin Luther.

**Lohr, 1588.** First Vespers of Sundays and feasts are sung in Latin, "according to the order
of Lossius's *Psalmodia*, as they are noted for every occasion". **Rieneck, *Vesperordnung zu
Lohr*, 1588** (Sehling 11, p. 699):

<!-- doc 318 -->
> (damit die jugent im psalliren und choralgesang, wie in allen kirchen gebreuchlich, geüebet
> werde) mit lateinischen psalmen, responsoriis, hymnis, Magnificat, collectis, versiculis,
> Benedicamus und anderm nach ordnung der psalmodiae L. Lossii, wie dieselben nach erheischung
> jederzeit notiert und bisher in brauch und uebung gewesen, gesungen und gehalten werden

(that the youth be exercised in psalmody and plainchant, as is customary in all churches) [it
shall] be sung and kept with Latin psalms, responsories, hymns, *Magnificat*, collects,
versicles, *Benedicamus* and the rest, according to the order of L. Lossius's *Psalmodia*, as
the same are noted for every occasion and have hitherto been in use and practice

Other orders cite Lossius too:
- **Hof 1592** cites antiphons "in Lossius's *Psalmodia*" and "in the great thin antiphoner"
  (Sehling 11, p. 422).
- **Lüneburg 1575** refers to "Lossius's book" for the festal Compline (Sehling 6/1, p. 658).
- **Buxtehude 1565** takes its noted pieces from Lossius's second edition
  (Sehling 7/1, p. 67, introduction).

#### <a id="s10-9-3"></a>10.9.3 German psalm tones

**Keppel, 1570.** The German office at Keppel is sung from the printed German psalm-books with
their notes. The preacher is to teach the nuns the melodies. **Nassau-Dillenburg, *Ordnung für
das Kloster Keppel*, 1570** (Sehling 10, p. 133):

<!-- doc 181 -->
> Es sollenn auch die zwen chore einen verß umb den andern singen unnd die tonos verendern, wie
