- **Gottleuba (1567):** "in the office they use lighted candles on the altar, chalice, paten,
  Mass vestment and all other ornaments" (Sehling 1, p. 567).
- **Danzig (1557):** the sexton is to watch "so long as the book, the can, the chalice and the
  paten stand on the altar", that no harm or theft befall them (Sehling 4, p. 214).
- **Strasbourg (1598):** a box with the particles, a can of wine, the chalice and the paten are
  set on the altar at the beginning of the service (Sehling 20/1, p. 611).

**In the hand at the Words of Institution.** The commonest rubric puts the paten, with as many
hosts as there are communicants, into the minister's hand while he says or sings the words over
the bread. **Kurpfalz, *Gemaine maß*, 1546** (Sehling 14, p. 97):

<!-- doc 472 -->
> Und wann er uf diese wort khompt: name er das brot, so nymbt er die paten, daruf die hostia
> alle liegen, sovil der communicanten, die sich dann zuvor angezeigt, absolvirt und zugelassen
> sein, in die hende und, wann die verba consecrationis vollendet sein, legt ers wider von sich.
> Deßgleichen thut er auch nachvolgents mit dem kelch

And when he cometh to these words, "he took the bread", he taketh the paten, on which lie all
the hosts, as many as there are communicants who have announced themselves beforehand, been
absolved and admitted, into his hands; and when the words of consecration are finished, he
layeth it away from him again. Likewise doth he afterwards also with the chalice.

The same rubric appears in many orders:
- **Livonia (1533):** the priest takes "the bread upon the paten into his hand", turns about
  over the altar toward the people, and speaks the words aloud (Sehling 5, p. 16).
- **Mecklenburg (1540/1545):** after the Lord's Prayer he "taketh the paten with the bread into
  his hand" and sings the Verba, turned toward the altar (Sehling 5, p. 154).
- **The *Cellische Ordnungen* (1545):** the priest lays "as many particles as belong to the
  communicants" in the paten, turns with it toward the people, and says the Verba in German
  (Sehling 1, p. 301).
- **Danzig (1557):** he takes "the paten with the appointed host into his hand without all
  papistical crossing and other gestures" (Sehling 4, p. 168).
- **Neuenrade (1564):** "he taketh the paten with the bread and turneth to the people"
  (Sehling 22, p. 519).
- **Schwarzburg (1574):** "he taketh the paten of the bread, wherein are as many particles as
  there are communicants" (Sehling 2, p. 133).
- **Henneberg (1582):** the minister shall "always have the paten with the particles in his
  hand" when he says "This is my body" (Sehling 2, p. 309).

The number of hosts on the paten was counted to the number of communicants. The Palatinate
(Reformed) wants nothing left over to be reserved (above). Württemberg in 1562 found the
minister in some places repeating the Verba "when there is no more bread and wine on the paten
and in the chalice", and in others not (Sehling 16, p. 436).

**Held under the chin.** At the sick communion of Brandenburg (1540) "the priest shall also
specially hold the paten cleanly under" as he gives the host (Sehling 3, p. 80). Pfalz-Neuburg
(1543) adds "that nothing fall" (Sehling 13, p. 88). The Palatine sick order of 1556 dropped the
instruction (editors' note, Sehling 14, p. 111). In the Mass the same office passed to the
communion cloth held by two men or boys ([§14.6.3](#s14-6-3)).

**Shown, and then not shown.** The paten could be shown to the people with the chalice.
Havelberg (1558) insists that the elevation of the sacrament remain, "much less shall the paten
be elevated in the stead of the chalice" (Sehling 3, p. 230). Hohenlohe abolished the showing in
1596. **Hohenlohe, *Verbesserungen der Kirchenzeremonien*, 1596** (Sehling 15, p. 659):

<!-- doc 628 -->
> Also auch die monstration belangend patinae et calicis under der recitation verborum coenae
> achten wir auch, dieweyl brott und wein in der handlung des abendmalls ohne das auf dem altar
> offentlich aufgestelt sind, das derowegen solche monstratio panis et vmi (weyl es unsere
> gnedige herrschaft je also haben will) soll eingestelt werden

So also concerning the showing of the paten and the chalice during the recitation of the words
of the Supper, we also judge, since bread and wine in the action of the Supper are in any case
set out openly on the altar, that therefore such showing of bread and wine (since our gracious
lordship will have it so) shall be given up.

Nassau-Weilburg's explanations of 1617 likewise call it "unnecessary that the minister, while he
speaketh the words of institution of the holy Supper, layeth hold of the paten and the chalice
severally", and order it stopped (Sehling 10, p. 351). At Hof, before Pangratius's time, the
deacon of the week broke his large host, "left a particle lying in the paten after the old
catholic custom", and after communion dropped it into the chalice (Sehling 11, p. 453).

**In the inventories.** Patens were counted with the chalices:
- Potsdam (1541): "2 patens" beside five chalices; at the chapel of St Gertrude "the patens and
  vestments are burnt" (Sehling 3, pp. 259–260);
- Oschatz (1555): "8 chalices with their patens" (Sehling 1, p. 628);
- Fürstenberg in Mecklenburg (1578): "two silver gilt patens" (Sehling 5, p. 265; [§14.6.6](#s14-6-6)).

The Merseburg visitors of 1544 asked what the church had "in store in patens, monstrances,
chalices and other silver" (Sehling 2, p. 12). Other orders charge the church officers with the
patens and other treasures:
- the *Altermann* of Ermsleben (1564) hands over "the treasures of chalices, patens, albs,
  chasubles" to his successors (Sehling 2, p. 488);
- Pfalz-Neuburg (1576) orders the church doors and windows barred "with strong grilles and iron
  bolts" for the sake of the "chalices, patens and other" treasures (Sehling 13, p. 207);
- the Sponheim visitation order of 1590/91 lists, among the things each church must have, "a
  chalice and a paten for the communion; a capsule or box for the wafers or hosts; a pewter can,
  or where needful two, for the wine" (Sehling 18, p. 655).

**The host box.** The particles were kept in a box (*Lade*, *Schachtel*, *Kapsel*): Sponheim and
Strasbourg (above; both Lutheran). The *ciborium* for reservation went with the monstrance:
Pomerania 1535 needs no ciborium (Sehling 4, p. 342), and Teschen 1584 names "the shutting of
the sacrament into the ciborium" among idolatrous ceremonies (Sehling 3, p. 461). Reservation is
treated in [§14.5.5](#s14-5-5).

**The Reformed dish.** The Reformed gave up the paten with the chalice:
- **Pfalz-Zweibrücken (1595, Reformed):** all chalices and patens were to be collected and made
  into beakers ([§14.6.5](#s14-6-5)).
- **Ysenburg-Birstein (1598, Reformed):** the ministers are not to use "consecrated chalices,
  patens and altars", but ordinary bread, broken and given into the hands, and "a clean drinking
  vessel" for the wine (Sehling 10, p. 645).
- **Wittgenstein (1605, Reformed):** the Mass vestments, patens and chalices are to be sold to
  advantage and a beaker bought for each place (Sehling 22, p. 149).
- **The dish.** In its place the bread was carried in a dish (*Schüssel*). Micron's London order
  (Reformed), printed with the Emden orders, passes the dishes with the bread among those
  sitting at the table (editors' comparison of the Supper forms, Sehling 7/1, p. 576). The
  Lutheran Marienhafe order of 1593 also names "table cloth, chalice, dish and can" for the
  Supper (Sehling 7/1, p. 710).

**Not found.** No order regulates the paten's material or size, or the veil and burse that go
with it. None mentions the paten's use at the offertory, or the minister's wiping of it.

---

### <a id="s14-7"></a>14.7 Vestments

#### <a id="s14-7-1"></a>14.7.1 The Mass vestment kept

**Allstedt 1533.** In Electoral Saxony the Lutheran visitors restored the Mass vestment where
radicals had dropped it. At Allstedt, where Müntzer (Radical Reformation) had celebrated in a
surplice or in ordinary clothes, pastors are to wear alb and chasuble "as is now done at
Allstedt and also at Wittenberg", with two burning lights. These ceremonies serve good
discipline and do no harm. **Allstedt, *Ordnung der Visitatoren*, 1533** (Sehling 1, p. 510):

<!-- doc 53 -->
> So auch etzliche bisanher ohne alben und casulen in einem korock, auch etzliche in schlechten
> kleidern mes gehalten, sollen sie furthin alben und casulen, wie itz zu Alstedt auch zu
> Wittenberg und anderswo gehalten wird, auch gebrauchen, darzu zwei brennende licht unter
> messen auch haben, dann diese ceremonien, welche zu ordnung guter zucht, dienen und
> unschedlich sein

Since also some until now have held Mass without albs and chasubles in a surplice, and some also
in plain clothes, they shall henceforth also use albs and chasubles, as is now kept at Allstedt
and also at Wittenberg and elsewhere, [and] have also two burning lights during Mass besides;
for these ceremonies, which serve for the order of good discipline and are harmless …

**Leisnig 1529.** At Leisnig, where for six years the pastors had consecrated "without surplice
and Mass vestment, simply in the coat", every pastor in the whole district is to use the Mass
vestment whenever he consecrates, conforming to Torgau and Wittenberg. **Leisnig, *Verordnung
der Visitatoren*, 1529** (Sehling 1, p. 605):

<!-- doc 103 -->
> die pfarrer und jenigen, so dem volk das sacrament geraicht, ane korrock und messgewand siecht
> im rock consecrirt, ist ernstlich bevolen, das forthin alle pfarrer nicht allein zu Leisnik
> sunder im ganzen kreis messgewand und andere unschedliche cerimonien, so oft sie consecriren,
> brauchen, und allenthalben nach dem buchlen der visitator, auch dem angefangnem brauch der
> kirchen zu Torgau und Wittemberg sich gleichformig machen sollen.

[whereas] the pastors and those who have reached the sacrament to the people have consecrated
without surplice and Mass vestment, simply in the coat, it is earnestly commanded that
henceforth all pastors, not only at Leisnig but in the whole district, use the Mass vestment and
other harmless ceremonies as oft as they consecrate, and everywhere conform themselves to the
booklet of the visitors and to the begun use of the churches at Torgau and Wittenberg.

**Calenberg 1544/45.** The Calenberg synods order the chasuble and two lights and abolish the
elevation, for uniformity and "for the simple and weak's sake". **Calenberg-Göttingen,
*Synodalkonstitutionen*, 1544/1545** (Sehling 6/2, p. 868):

<!-- doc 2038 -->
> setzen demnach und ordenen, das die celebratio coenae dominicae nicht anders, dann in der
> ordenunge vermeldet, gehalten, die elevatio gar abgeschafft, die mesgewender oder casel
> angezogen und 2 liechte auf den altar gesetzt werden sollen, nicht, das an solchen ceremonien
> etwas sonderlichs gelegen sey, sonder das wir gerne eine gleicheit und ehrbarkeit umb der
> einfeltigen und schwachen willen

[we] appoint therefore and ordain that the celebration of the Lord's Supper be held no otherwise
than is set forth in the order; the elevation wholly abolished; the Mass vestments or chasuble
put on; and two lights set upon the altar: not that anything special lieth on such ceremonies,
but that we would gladly [have] a uniformity and seemliness for the simple and weak's sake.

**Wolfenbüttel 1569.** The Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel order requires the ministers, when there are
communicants, to come to the altar "not only in their customary clothes" but in their church
ornaments. **Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, *Kirchenordnung*, 1569** (Sehling 6/1, p. 143):

<!-- doc 1974 -->
> pastores und kirchendiener, so messe halten wöllen, wenn communicanten vorhanden sein, nicht
> bloß mit ihren gewönlichen kleidern, sondern in ihrem ornatu ecclesiastico, als alben, caseln
> und meßgewand fein ehrlich und mit grosser andacht und anruffung des Sons Gottes vor den altar
> tretten und das officium missae anfahen, halten und verrichten.

pastors and ministers who will hold Mass, when communicants are present, [shall] step before the
altar not merely in their customary clothes but in their church ornaments, as albs, chasubles
and Mass vestment, finely and honestly and with great devotion and calling upon the Son of God,
and begin, hold and perform the office of the Mass.

**Grubenhagen 1544.** Grubenhagen orders alb and chasuble and lights at the Sacrament, "to the
honour of the sacrament", and the surplice for all other offices in church. **Grubenhagen,
*Kirchenordnung*, 1544** (Sehling 6/2, p. 1032):

<!-- doc 2056 -->
> III. Vom kleyde und lichtern, die man zum sacrament gebrauchen sol. Und in solcher
> administrirung der heiligen sacramenta solen die pfarhern dem sacrament zu ehren alven und
> kassel anziehen und licht auf dem altar brennen, auch in deutsche sprache die episteln und
> evangelia mit einem gewonlichen accentu singen, aber ausserhalbe dem ampte in der kirchen
> sollen der pfarher und opperman ihre korrock anhaben und gebrauchen.

III. Of the clothing and lights which one shall use for the sacrament. And in such administering
of the holy sacraments the pastors shall, to the honour of the sacrament, put on alb and
chasuble and [have] lights burn upon the altar, and also sing the epistles and gospels in the
German language with a customary accent; but outside the office in the church the pastor and the
sexton shall have on and use their surplices.

Thorn 1575 has the priests minister "in the customary church clothes, chasuble and surplice"
([§14.6.3](#s14-6-3)), and Thüngen 1564 keeps the Mass vestment for peace ([§14.3.3](#s14-3-3)). Hildesheim 1544 keeps
vestments and lights but leaves stole and maniple free ([§14.3.3](#s14-3-3)).

**Riga 1530.** The Riga order makes the variation itself a lesson in freedom: a plain surplice
on Sundays, a cope or chasuble over it on high feasts, since there are still plenty of them,
"that one may see that neither this nor that is needful". **Riga, *Kirchenordnung*, 1530**
(Sehling 5, p. 17):

<!-- doc 1897 -->
> Auf die fest aber, mag er ein chorkappe oder casel (die weil ihr noch genug verhanden ist, und
> doch sonst, wiewol sie viel gelt gekost haben, da verterben) schlecht über das röckel ziehen,
> auf das durch solche stete verwandlung und enderung die freiheit solcher eusserlichen ding,
> destebas vermerckt werd, auf das man sehe, das wider dis noch jens nötig sei, und das eben so
> wenig an schwarze oder blaue röckel, als wenig als an chorröckel oder chormentel oder casel,
> die freiheit des evangeliums gebunden

But on the feasts he may simply draw a cope or chasuble over the little surplice (since there
are still enough of them, and otherwise, though they have cost much money, they spoil there),
that by such constant change and alteration the freedom of such outward things may be the better
perceived; that one may see that neither this nor that is needful, and that the freedom of the
gospel is bound as little to black or blue coats as to surplices or copes or chasubles.

**Kurland 1570.** Kurland follows Riga: a white linen garment or surplice at the altar, any
festal vestment allowed on high feasts, none in the pulpit. **Kurland, *Kirchenordnung*, 1570**
(Sehling 5, p. 99):

<!-- doc 1907 -->
> demnach sollen die priester nach altem, löblichen, gebliebenem gebrauch dieser kirchen für dem
> altar, wenn sie des sontags oder zu andern zeiten die communion halten, in einem weissen,
> leinen kleide oder chor röcklein verkleidet, dem altar dienen […] Wenn man aber auf die
> obnangezeigten hohen festen zur verendrung andere seitgewant, caseln, mesgewand, priesterliche
> kleidung und dergleichen wil für dem altar gebrauchen, ist auch niemands verboten. Auf der
> canzel aber sol man keine verkleidung, darum das es in diesen landen nach der Rijgischen
> kirchenordnung ungewöntlich, gebrauchen.

therefore the priests, according to the old, laudable, remaining use of this church, shall serve
the altar before the altar, when they hold the communion on Sunday or at other times, clad in a
white linen garment or little surplice […] But if on the aforesaid high feasts one will use
before the altar, for a change, other silken vestments, chasubles, Mass vestment, priestly
clothing and the like, it is also forbidden to no one. But in the pulpit one shall use no
vesting, because it is unaccustomed in these lands according to the Riga church order.

#### <a id="s14-7-2"></a>14.7.2 The cope when there is no communion

Where there were no communicants, several orders forbade the chasuble, so that the people should
not think the private Mass had returned. The minister wore a cope or a surplice instead.
**Pfalz-Neuburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1543** (Sehling 13, p. 77):

<!-- doc 386 -->
> so sol der priester nit in gewonlichem meßgewand, sonder in einem chormantel oder nur in
> seinem chorrock für den altar treten und es aller ding halten, wie oben gesetzt ist

then the priest shall step before the altar not in the customary Mass vestment, but in a cope or
only in his surplice, and keep all things as is set above.

**Brandenburg, *Kirchen-ordnung*, 1540** (Sehling 3, p. 71):

<!-- doc 1746 -->
> Es sollen auch, wenn solche empter gehalten werden, die priester kein casula, sondern allein
> ein korkappen oder auf den dörfern, do die korkappen nicht weren, ein schlechten korrock
> anhaben, damit das einfeltig volk nicht auf voriger meinung bleib oder geleitet werde, als
> wolt man die mess nach voriger weiss mit der communion on communicanten widerum anheben und
> halten

The priests also, when such offices are held, shall have on no chasuble, but only a cope, or in
the villages, where there were no copes, a plain surplice; that the simple people abide not in,
nor be led into, the former opinion, as though one would begin and hold again the Mass after the
former manner, with the communion without communicants.

**Schwäbisch Hall 1527.** Brenz allows the deacon a cope at the common prayer, so that church
vesture be not wholly rejected, but not a Mass vestment, "for it is neither a man's nor a
woman's clothing". **Schwäbisch Hall, *Kirchenordnung*, 1527** (Sehling 17/1, p. 50):

<!-- doc 755 -->
> Und das die kirchencleydung nit gar verworffen werde, mocht der diaconus, so sich bezimen
> wolt, des gebets ernst und herlichait zuerzaigen, ain Cormantel anlegen, wie bißhieher zu
> vesper und metten gewont war, aber nit ein meßgewandt, dan es kein mans noch weybs claidung
> ist, sonder zu gar nerrisch anzusehen vor der gemeinen versamlung.

And that church vesture be not wholly rejected, the deacon, if it would beseem him to show forth
the earnestness and majesty of the prayer, might put on a cope, as hitherto was the custom at
Vespers and Matins; but not a Mass vestment, for it is neither a man's nor a woman's clothing,
but altogether too foolish to look upon before the common assembly.

#### <a id="s14-7-3"></a>14.7.3 Vestments abolished

**Dalmatic and tunicle.** The Homberg synod of 1526 (Moderate Reformed) forbids the vestments of
deacons and subdeacons outright, since it will not favour orders without warrant in God's word.
**Hesse, *Homberger Kirchenordnung*, 1526** (Moderate Reformed; Sehling 8, p. 46):

<!-- doc 2247 -->
> [24] Dalmaticas, hoc est papisticorum diaconorum vestes aut subdiaconorum nemo de caetero
> induat. Nolumus enim favere ordinibus illis sine Dei eloquiorum testimoniis

[24] Dalmatics, that is, the vestments of the papistical deacons or subdeacons, let no one put
on henceforth. For we will not favour those orders without the testimonies of the oracles of
God.

**Regensburg 1554.** The fullest statement of reasons in the corpus is Regensburg's, written by
Nikolaus Gallus to be read from the pulpit, on why the "Levite and Mass vestments" are to go.
First, both come from the Levitical priesthood and the papal Mass. **Regensburg, *Warum die
leviten- und meßgewand sollen abgetan werden*, 29 April 1554** (Sehling 13, p. 432):

<!-- doc 443 -->
> Ein ehrbar rat hat sampt uns dienern des worts für gut angesehen, das die leviten- und
> meßgewand bei der communion in unser christlichen kirchen alhie wie bei vielen andern hinfort
> genzlich abgetan sein sollen. Dasselbig aus nachvolgenden ursachen: Erstlich, das beide stück
> (wie zum teil die namen noch anzeigen) vom levitischen priestertum des alten testaments und
> von des bapsts messe in unser kirchen kommen und ihre bedeutung auf den zukünftigen Christum
> gehabt haben.

An honourable council together with us ministers of the word hath thought good that the Levite
and Mass vestments at the communion in our Christian church here, as with many others, shall
henceforth be wholly put away. The same for the following causes: First, that both pieces (as
the names in part still show) have come into our church from the Levitical priesthood of the Old
Testament and from the pope's Mass, and have had their signification upon the Christ to come.

Second, the pope still requires them as necessary. Third, they hinder the simple and make it
look as if there were little difference between the papal and the evangelical service. Anyone
still offended after so many years of teaching "is hardly any more to be counted among the
weak". The surplice stays, but only as a mark of the minister. **Regensburg, *Warum die leviten-
und meßgewand sollen abgetan werden*, 29 April 1554** (Sehling 13, p. 433):

<!-- doc 444 -->
> Doch lassen wir leviten- und meßgewand also fallen, das wir noch zur zeit den chorrock lassen
> bleiben, wie wir ihn bisher haben behalten aus freiem willen weder umb des bapstes oder
> interims willen noch, das er ichts zum gottesdienst nötig sein sölte, sondern allein zu
> unterscheid der diener, dieweil sie da im ampt stehen und zwischen der andern gemeine

Yet we let the Levite and Mass vestments so fall, that we still for the time let the surplice
remain, as we have kept it hitherto of free will, neither for the pope's nor for the Interim's
sake, nor that it should be anything needful to the service of God, but only for a difference of
the ministers, while they stand there in office, and the rest of the congregation.

The Regensburg order of [1567] repeats the reasons and adds the stole and the lights.
**Regensburg, *Kirchenordnung*, [1567]** (Sehling 13, p. 480):

<!-- doc 450 -->
> Demnach haben wir auch die kirchenkleidung, als meßgewand, stolen, leviten usw. gleich wie
> auch die liechter, so von anfang der reinen lere gleichwol lange zeit in unser pfarrhe mit
> gehalten worden, entlich sampt den obgemelten, etlichen feiertägen lassen fallen aus ursachen,
> das die ding aus dem alten testament von dem levitischen priestertum, so sein ende hat, mit
> unverstand sind in das neue testament eingefürt und in eitel bapstisch abgötterei gewendet.

Accordingly we have also at last let fall the church vesture, as Mass vestment, stoles, Levite
[vestments], etc., even as also the lights, which nevertheless from the beginning of the pure
doctrine were kept a long time in our parish, together with some of the aforesaid feast days,
for the causes that these things were brought without understanding out of the Old Testament,
from the Levitical priesthood, which hath its end, into the New Testament, and turned into mere
popish idolatry.

**Transylvania 1557.** The Hermannstadt synod holds that burning candles, *infulae* and
ornaments, though indifferent in themselves, have ceased to be indifferent because so many
churches have cast them out as popish dregs. They are to be laid aside in time, once the people
are taught. A seemly white linen garment without images may serve instead. **Hermannstadt,
*Synodalbeschlüsse*, 1557** (Sehling 24, p. 262):

<!-- doc 1675 -->
> Incensio candelarum, infulae et ornatus, etiam si res mediae sint et per se neque prosint
> neque obsint, tamen cum plurimae ecclesiae eas ut feces Papisticas abiecerint et nunc sine
> scandalo retineri non possint ac in numero rerum mediarum propter hoc accidens esse desierint,
> successu temporis, ubi populus edoctus fuerit, verum usum sacramenti non in ista specie
> externa et fulgente consistere […] abiici debent. Cum autem sine aliquo decoro speciali haec
> actio sacra et gravissima peragi non possit, linea veste alba decente, carente idolis id fieri
> potest, ut ex primitivae ecclesiae testimonio manifestum est.

The burning of candles, *infulae* and ornaments, even if they be indifferent things and of
themselves neither profit nor hurt, yet since very many churches have cast them away as popish
dregs, and they cannot now be retained without offence, and by this accident have ceased to be
in the number of indifferent things, ought to be cast away in course of time, when the people
shall have been taught that the true use of the sacrament consisteth not in that outward and
shining show […]. But since this sacred and most weighty action cannot be performed without some
special seemliness, it may be done in a seemly white linen garment, void of images, as is
manifest from the testimony of the primitive church.

*Infula* here most likely means the chasuble, as in other Transylvanian and Hungarian usage, not
the mitre.

**Others.** The Sayn synod of 1575 drops the Mass vestment and keeps the surplice
(Sehling 19/1, p. 356). Anhalt 1596 (Reformed) orders "Mass vestment and chasubles" laid aside
([§14.5.2](#s14-5-2)), and the Lutheran Sponheim 1590/91 turns them into altar cloths ([§14.6.1](#s14-6-1)).

#### <a id="s14-7-4"></a>14.7.4 The surplice

**The minimum.** Where nothing else survived, the surplice (*Chorrock*) usually did. It is the
vestment most often named in the corpus, and the reasons given for it are always the same: to
distinguish the minister in office from the congregation, and to keep the service seemly. Duke
Albrecht's Prussian ordinance of 1543 forbids any pastor to preach, baptize or give the
sacraments without at least a white surplice. **Prussia, *Befehl*, 1 February 1543**
(Sehling 4, p. 60):

<!-- doc 1833 -->
> kein predig thun, taufen oder sacramenta reichen, es sei dann, sie haben zum wenigsten einen
> weissen chorrock an, domit dannoch hierinnen auch eusserlich ein weltlicher unterscheid
> zwischen dem diener des worts, wann er in seinem ambt ist, und einem andern, der nicht darzu
> berufen, zu sehen.

[shall] do no preaching, baptizing or reaching of sacraments, unless they have on at the least a
white surplice, that so herein also outwardly a worldly difference may be seen between the
minister of the word, when he is in his office, and another who is not called thereto.

**Hesse 1532** (Moderate Reformed). The Hessian order uses the surplice "for the people's sake",
to revive a reverence "almost wholly extinguished". **Hesse, *Ordenung der Christlichen
kirchen*, 1532** (Moderate Reformed; Sehling 8, p. 76):

<!-- doc 2252 -->
> und, wen es versamlet ist, ists umb des volks willen fur geschickt angesehen (ut vel sic
> quodam modo plebis reverentiam pene prorsus extinctam alamus), einen chorock zu brauchen

and, when it is assembled, it is thought fit for the people's sake (*that even so we may in some
manner nourish the reverence of the common people, almost wholly extinguished*) to use a
surplice.

**Württemberg 1535.** The preface to the Württemberg order of 1535 grants that clothing makes no
man godly or ungodly, but rules the surplice in for all church offices. It is "not the least
outward ornament of the church" that the minister be known by an honest, distinct garment. Many
weak believers had been put off the gospel by seeing ministers stand "in a stumpy little coat".
**Württemberg, *Vorrede zur Kirchenordnung*, 1535** (Sehling 16, p. 133):

<!-- doc 652 -->
> Von der klaidung im kirchenampt. Die kleidung macht an ir selbs weder frum noch unfrum unnd
> wurdt under die freyen stuck gezelet. […] so soll fürohin alwegen in den kirchen emptern der
> Chorrock gebraucht werden. Dan dieweyll alles in der kirchen zierlich und ordenlich zu ghen
> soll, so ist es nicht die geringst eusserlich kirchen zier, das der jenig, so im brauch des
> kirchenampts vor der gemeinen kirchen versamblung stheet, bey einem erbarn underschidlichen
> claid erkennet werde. Darzu ists offenbar, das vill schwach glaubige on andere ursach, auch
> von wegen diser ursach, das sie den kirchendienern on biß anher gewonliche kirchen cleidern
> allein in einem stumpfen rocklin in den emptern sehen sthen, ein mercklich abscheuhen von der
> predig des hailgen evangelium, auch von brauch der sacramenten uber komen.

Of the clothing in the church office. Clothing of itself maketh neither godly nor ungodly, and
is reckoned among the free things. […] so shall henceforth the surplice be used always in the
church offices. For since all things in the church should go comely and in order, it is not the
least outward ornament of the church that he who standeth before the common assembly of the
church in the exercise of the church office be known by an honest, distinct garment. Moreover it
is manifest that many weak in faith, for no other cause but this cause also, that they see the
ministers standing in the offices without the hitherto customary church clothes, only in a
stumpy little coat, have gotten a notable abhorrence of the preaching of the holy gospel and
also of the use of the sacraments.

The great Württemberg order of 1553 confirms it "until our further decision". **Württemberg,
*Kirchenordnung*, 1553** (Sehling 16, p. 266):

<!-- doc 671 -->
> So mögen wir leiden, das die kirchendiener in allen ämptern, so sie in der kirchen verrichten
> sollen, den gwonlichen Chorrock biß auff ferner unsern bescheid gebrauchen und sonst auch in
> allweg sich einer ehrlichen, gebürlichen kleidung fleissigen, damit nicht allein ir wort und
> predig, sonder auch ir kleidung, weiß und geberde ein leer der tugendt seien.

So may we suffer that the ministers in all offices which they are to perform in the church use
the customary surplice until our further decision, and otherwise also in every way study an
honest, seemly clothing, that not only their word and preaching but also their clothing, manner
and bearing may be a teaching of virtue.

**The Cellische Ordnungen 1545.** The Albertine Saxon ordinances of 1545 make it a rule of
clerical discipline. **Albertine Saxony, *Die Cellischen Ordnungen*, 1545** (Sehling 1, p. 302):

<!-- doc 33 -->
> 2. In ubunge gotlicher ampter in der kirchen söllen die priester allewege ein chorrock
> anhaben, dan es sol in der kirchen decenter venuste et honeste zugehen.

2. In the exercise of divine offices in the church the priests shall always have on a surplice,
   for in the church things shall go decently, comely and honestly.

**Wittgenstein 1563.** Wittgenstein leaves the old vestments free but keeps the surplice "with
one accord", since a minister should be somewhat distinguished from others in his clothing.
**Wittgenstein, *Kirchenordnung*, 1563** (Sehling 22, p. 97):

<!-- doc 1493 -->
> Dieweil es aber gleichwoll billich und ehrlich ist, das ein kirchendiener sein ampt züchtig
> vor der gemeine verrichte und in der kleidung von andern etwas underschieden werde, soll man
> den chorrock darzu eintrechtiglich erhalten und brauchen. Und sollen die pastores sampt den
> kirchenmeistern versehung thun, das die gebreuchliche kirchen ornamenta bestellet und sauber
> gehalten werden.

But since it is nevertheless meet and honest that a minister perform his office modestly before
the congregation and be somewhat distinguished from others in his clothing, one shall keep and
use the surplice thereto with one accord. And the pastors together with the churchwardens shall
take order that the customary church ornaments be provided and kept clean.

**Anhalt 1568.** In Anhalt the surplice is worn at all three Sunday sermons and may be left off
on weekdays. **Anhalt, *Abschied* of Prince Bernhard, 1568** (Sehling 2, p. 570):

<!-- doc 1262 -->
> desgleichen soll des sontags zu allen dreien predigten der chorrock gebraucht, die wochen uber
> auch nachgelassen werden.

likewise the surplice shall be used on Sunday at all three sermons, and over the week also be
let go.

**Limited.** In Ernestine Saxony after 1554 the surplice was dropped in the pulpit but kept at
the altar. **Ernestine Saxony, *Instruction* of the dukes, 1554** (Sehling 1, p. 224):

<!-- doc 21 -->
> idoch solle der chorock auf der canzel zugebrauchen in alwege und an allen orten durchaus
> abgeschaft, aber von dem altar unter der sacrament raichung nochglassen werden

yet the use of the surplice in the pulpit shall be abolished in every way and in all places
throughout, but at the altar during the reaching of the sacrament be permitted.

Coburg in the same year limits it to the communion, worn only by the one who celebrates.
**Coburg, *Vorschaffung*, 1554** (Sehling 1, p. 544):

<!-- doc 74 -->
> Zum sechsten der chorock sol wider zu den begrebnussen noch auf der canzel noch sonsten in
> andern kirchenampten, sondern allain zur communion von der ainigen person welche das ampt
> heldet, gebraucht werden.

Sixthly, the surplice shall be used neither at burials nor in the pulpit nor otherwise in other
church offices, but only at the communion, by the one person who holdeth the office.

**Abolished.** The Palatine Calvinists abolished the surplice with the communion cloth at Amberg
in 1567 (Reformed), and the Lutheran Upper Palatine visitation of 1579 dropped both again under
Ludwig VI ([§14.6.3](#s14-6-3)). The Sayn consistory did the same in 1582, in the same protocol that orders the
remaining images removed (Sehling 19/1, p. 377).

**The black gown.** The Wild- und Rheingrafschaft order of 1603 is the only order found that
prescribes a black gown. Each minister is to have a black church gown with sleeves made "at the
first opportunity" and wear it in his office. White surplices are to be kept where they are in
use, without superstition, and not abolished without the count's knowledge. **Wild- und
Rheingrafschaft, *Kirchenordnung*, 1603** (Sehling 19/2, p. 630):

<!-- doc 1121 -->
> Beßonders aber wollen wir, daß jeder unßerer kirchendiener erster gelegenheit nach ihme ein
> schwartzen kirchenrock mit ermeln zeuge und in verrichtunge seines ampts anziehe. Waß aber die
> weiße chorröck anlangett, wo dieselbige in unßern kirchen in usurpantz und gebräuchlich sein,
> da soll man solche ohn superstition oder aberglauben behalten und ohn unßer vorwißen nit
> abschaffen.

But especially we will that each of our ministers at the first opportunity get himself a black
church gown with sleeves, and put it on in the performing of his office. But as for the white
surplices, where the same are in practice and use in our churches, there shall one keep them
without superstition or superstitious belief, and not abolish them without our knowledge.

#### <a id="s14-7-5"></a>14.7.5 What the orders do not mention

The orders never mention the amice, cincture, maniple (except to leave it free at Hildesheim),
tunicle (except under "Levite vestments"), humeral veil, rochet, biretta, zucchetto, galero,
pallium, rationale, episcopal gloves, tippet or hood, nor any preaching bands. No evangelical
order provides a mitre or crosier, and none prescribes liturgical colours ([§14.6.6](#s14-6-6)). See [§14.2.3](#s14-2-3).

---

### <a id="s14-8"></a>14.8 Clerical dress outside the service

**Long priestly coats.** The orders want the minister to be recognisable in the street as well
as in church. Grubenhagen 1544 adds to its rule on vestments ([§14.7.1](#s14-7-1)) that pastors are otherwise
to go in long priestly coats. **Grubenhagen, *Kirchenordnung*, 1544** (Sehling 6/2, p. 1032):

<!-- doc 2056 -->
> Sonsten sollen sie in zimlichen, ehrlichen, langen pristerlichen rocken oder kleydungen ghan
> und nicht hertretten wie landsknechte und andere wilde junge leute.

Otherwise they shall go in seemly, honest, long priestly coats or clothing, and not stride along
like soldiers and other wild young people.

The Albertine ordinances of 1545 give the same rule more fully. **Albertine Saxony, *Die
Cellischen Ordnungen*, 1545** (Sehling 1, p. 302):

<!-- doc 33 -->
> 1. Die priester söllen eherliche lange cleider tragen, nicht also verkürzt und verstummelt,
> wie die leichtfertigen leute einher gehen, auch nicht zur schnitten ader bunte kleider tragen
> und in götlichen ampten keine ausgeschnittene schue tragen, die do ergerlich seind.

1. The priests shall wear honest long clothes, not so shortened and docked as the light-minded
   folk go about, nor wear slashed or coloured clothes, and in divine offices wear no cut-out
   shoes, which are offensive.

**To be known.** Regensburg [1567], which kept the surplice so that ministers in office might be
known, adds that "outside the office also they should have their honest, priestly clothing for
distinction's sake". **Regensburg, *Kirchenordnung*, [1567]** (Sehling 13, p. 481):

<!-- doc 450 -->
> auch darumb, das die kirchendiener, wenn sie in ihrem ampt sind, in und für der andern gemein
> dester mehr erkent werden, wie sie sonst auch außer dem ampt unterscheids halben ihre
> ehrliche, priesterliche kleidung haben söllen.

also for this cause, that the ministers, when they are in their office, may be the more known in
and before the rest of the congregation, as they should also otherwise, outside the office, have
their honest, priestly clothing for distinction's sake.

The Wild- und Rheingrafschaft order of 1603, which introduced the black gown ([§14.7.4](#s14-7-4)), says the
same. **Wild- und Rheingrafschaft, *Kirchenordnung*, 1603** (Sehling 19/2, p. 630):

<!-- doc 1121 -->
> Dann obwohl die kleidung in der kirchen, auch außerhalb derselben, keinen menschen weder
> heiliger noch unheiliger machen, jedoch weil alles ehrlich unndt zierlich zugehen soll,
> demnach wollen wir, daß unßere kirchendiener in undt außer ihrem ampt sich also mit kleidung
> tragen, daß dem ansehen deß ministerii und kirchendieners, so viel möglich, nichts benohmen
> werde.

For although clothing in the church, and also outside it, maketh no man either holier or
unholier, yet because all things should go honestly and comely, therefore we will that our
ministers, in and outside their office, so bear themselves in clothing that nothing be taken
from the dignity of the ministry and of the minister, so far as is possible.

Württemberg 1553 asks the same "honest, seemly clothing", so that the ministers' dress, manner
and bearing may be "a teaching of virtue" ([§14.7.4](#s14-7-4)). Riga 1530 reminds them that the gospel is not
bound to "black or blue coats" any more than to surplices ([§14.7.1](#s14-7-1)).

**Related.** Freiberg 1537 abolishes "wearing tonsures [and] cowls" among the merely human
ordinances, and Brunswick 1528 wants no tonsure and no special coat for deacons (see
[Chapter 16](#ch16), [§16.3.3](#s16-3-3)).

The conduct required of ministers and their households is treated in
[Chapter 15](#ch15), [§15.3.3](#s15-3-3).

---

## <a id="ch15"></a>Chapter 15. Ecclesiastical Duties in the Sehling Church Orders


This guide sets out what the evangelical church orders of the sixteenth century, printed in Emil
Sehling's *Die evangelischen Kirchenordnungen des XVI. Jahrhunderts*, required of each estate in
the church. It asks:

- **Clergy.** What were pastors and deacons, superintendents, members and presidents of
  consistories, and professors of theology expected or required to do?
- **Training.** How were ministers trained: school, university and stipend, practice preaching,
  examination, a probationary period, and continuing study after ordination?
- **Laity.** What did the orders require of ordinary church members: attendance, prayer at home,
  confession and communion? Were sextons, schoolmasters and other church workers held to a
  higher standard?
- **Schoolmasters.** What were their church duties?
- **The magistrate.** What were the prince's and the council's duties towards the church?
- **Catechesis.** How often was the catechism taught, and for how long? What did it require? Was
  first communion separate from confirmation, and did each require instruction? Did any order
  give communion to infants? Was there catechesis or counselling before marriage?

**How the guide is laid out.**
- [§15.1](#s15-1) answers each question in brief, and [§15.2](#s15-2) sets out the scope, the sources and the negative
  findings.
- §§[15.3](#s15-3)–[15.6](#s15-6) cover the clergy:
  - [§15.3](#s15-3), pastors and deacons;
  - [§15.4](#s15-4), superintendents and deans;
  - [§15.5](#s15-5), consistories, their presidents and members;
  - [§15.6](#s15-6), professors of theology.
- [§15.7](#s15-7) covers the training of ministers.
- [§15.8](#s15-8) covers the laity and the church workers.
- [§15.9](#s15-9) covers schoolmasters, and [§15.10](#s15-10) the magistrate.
- [§15.11](#s15-11) covers catechesis, where all the estates meet: its frequency and length, first communion,
  confirmation, instruction before marriage, and infant communion.
- [§15.12](#s15-12) is a table by order, and [§15.13](#s15-13) a concordance of every order quoted.

**Related guides.** Several subjects are treated more fully elsewhere and are only cited here:
- preaching and the catechism sermon: [Chapter 11](#ch11);
- the daily office and the obligations of clergy and students to it:
  [Chapter 10](#ch10), [§10.6](#s10-6);
- confirmation, marriage, ordination, installation, sextons, schoolmasters and magistrates as
  rites: [Chapter 13](#ch13), §§[13.6](#s13-6), [13.7](#s13-7), [13.10](#s13-10)–[13.13](#s13-13);
- deacons, elders and the minor offices:
  [Chapter 16](#ch16);
- the oaths and confessional subscriptions of ministers:
  [Chapter 17](#ch17);
- clerical dress: [Chapter 14](#ch14), [§14.8](#s14-8);
- the catechism service, its hour, length and order: [Chapter 10](#ch10),
  [§10.10](#s10-10);
- private confession and the examination of communicants:
  [Chapter 13](#ch13), [§13.17](#s13-17);
- the hearers during the sermon: [Chapter 11](#ch11), [§11.12](#s11-12).

**Conventions**

- **Quotations.** Every quotation is Sehling's text as it stands in the `eko.db` database built
  from the digitized edition.
  - Footnote numbers, sigla, folio markers and interleaved apparatus are left out.
  - Sehling's own supplied words in square brackets are kept, as are "[!]" and his other signs.
  - Spelling and punctuation are as printed, including plain OCR errors.
  - "[…]" marks an omission.
  - Every quotation has been checked against the database text, allowing for OCR noise: at least
    90 per cent of its words must be found there in order. Its page has been checked against the
    edition's page markers.
  - Each quotation is preceded by an HTML comment, invisible when rendered, that names the
    `eko.db` document it was checked against.
- **Translations.** The English is formal-equivalence, in the idiom of the Authorized Version:
  - Word order and clause structure are kept where English allows.
  - Stock terms are rendered the same way throughout. *Pfarrer* and *Pfarrherr* are "pastor";
    *Kirchendiener* is "minister of the church"; *Superattendent* and *Superintendent* are
    "superintendent"; *Kirchner*, *Küster*, *Custos* and *Opfermann* are "sexton"; *Hausvater*
    is "householder"; *Gesinde* is "servants"; *Verhör* and *examen* are "examination";
    *aufbieten* and *proclamieren* are "proclaim" (the banns); *copulieren* and *einsegnen* are
    "marry" and "bless".
  - Words the translation supplies are in square brackets.
- **Citations.** Citations are in the form "Sehling volume, page".
  - The half-volumes of the edition are written 6/1, 6/2, 7/1, 7/2.1, 7/2.2, 17/1, 17/2, 19/1,
    19/2, 20/1 and 20/2, following the digitized volumes.
  - Each order is named by place, title and date as they appear in Sehling's running heads,
    which sometimes differ from the database's record headings. Where a passage is Sehling's own
    introduction or note, this is said.
- **Traditions.** Most of the orders cited are Lutheran, and they are not marked. Every order of
  another tradition is marked where it is cited, by its name in brackets after the order, as
  "Kurpfalz 1563 (Reformed)". The traditions follow the inventory in
  [Chapter 1](#ch1), [§1.3](#s1-3):
  - **Reformed**: the Swiss, Calvinist and Heidelberg churches, among them the German
    territories that turned Reformed after 1560 and the French and Dutch stranger churches;
  - **Moderate Reformed**: the Bucerian and related orders that stood between the Lutheran and
    the Swiss Reformed: Bucer's Strasbourg and the Upper German cities before the Interim,
    Philip of Hesse's church to 1566, Hermann von Wied's Cologne order, and Colmar after 1578;
  - **Philippist**: the churches that held to Melanchthon's later teaching and his *Corpus
    doctrinae* and refused the Formula of Concord: the joint Hessian synods and orders of
    1568–1598, Bremen 1556–1575, Nassau-Dillenburg 1575 and Anhalt 1590–1594.
  - The mark follows the order cited, not the territory, since a territory could change its
    tradition: Nassau-Dillenburg is Lutheran to 1570, Philippist in 1575 and Reformed from 1581.
  - The Transylvanian Saxons' own orders and synods are Lutheran; only the diet decrees of the
    principality are multi-confessional.

### <a id="s15-1"></a>15.1 Summary of findings

**1. Pastors: preach, administer, catechize, visit, study, and live as an example** ([§15.3](#s15-3)). The
visitation questions sum up the office: preaching, the sacraments, the catechism, weddings, and
visiting the sick and sorrowful (Strasbourg 1598). The pastor's other duties:
- **study** a set list of books: the Bible, Luther's postil, Melanchthon's *Loci* and the
  Augsburg Confession, with copies bought for every parish (Saxony 1557; Hoya 1581);
- **marry**, keep out of taverns and trade, and bring up wife, children and servants as a model
  household, which the visitors inspected;
- **reside**, never leaving the parish overnight without leave and a substitute (Hoya 1581);
- **keep registers** of baptisms, marriages and burials from mid-century (Saxony 1580).

The deacons had the catechism and the sick as their particular charges, "readier to serve the
poor herein than the rich" (Saxony 1555).

**2. Superintendents: visit, hold synod, examine, report** ([§15.4](#s15-4)). The Saxon pattern of 1555–1557
gives the superintendent four tasks:
- to watch over the doctrine, life and diligence of the pastors;
- to visit unannounced, hearing sermons and examining the youth;
- to hold a synod every year between Easter and Whitsun;
- to examine and install new pastors, and send to the consistory what he cannot mend.

By 1600 the superintendent was sworn to the confessional corpus and acted as the consistory's
agent (Grubenhagen). In Transylvania the chapters elected their own deans (Lasseln 1572).

**3. Consistories: theologians and jurists; the president disputed** ([§15.5](#s15-5)). The consistory judged
marriage cases, church discipline "so far as the degrees of admonition" go, the affairs of
ministers, and church property (Saxony 1580). The orders differed over who should preside:
- the prince in person (Weimar 1561);
- the superintendent (Jena 1569);
- a nobleman (Dresden 1580);
- a lay councillor, so that the clergy should not seem to "lay hold on the worldly sword … like
  the Pope" (Regensburg 1588).

The consistories met weekly and were sworn to secrecy.

**4. Professors: no seminaries** ([§15.6](#s15-6)). No order founds a seminary. Professors of theology appear
in the orders as members of consistories, as examiners and ordainers (Wittenberg, Leipzig,
Marburg, Helmstedt), as overseers of the stipendiaries, and as public lecturers.

**5. Training: stipend, practice sermon, examination, probation, synod** ([§15.7](#s15-7)). There was no
vicarage year, but training had parts that did similar work:
- stipends for poor students, bound to serve the territory;
- the Tübingen *Stipendium* (1559), where masters preached in the house and were corrected "*in
  inventione, dispositione oder pronunciatione*" the same day;
- practice sermons in the parish with the pastor's leave (Saxony 1555);
- examination and a trial sermon before ordination, and if needed some weeks of instruction at
  Wittenberg or Marburg;
- a probation as deacon before a parish, with a re-examination (Palatinate 1564, Reformed), and
  the new deacons' sermon outlines sent in for criticism after a year (Palatinate 1607,
  Reformed).

After ordination the synods set reading "that the priests may be moved the more diligently to
read and the sooner to buy books" (Nassau 1552). The Reformed monthly convents criticized each
member's sermon and disputed theological questions (Palatinate 1571, Reformed).

**6. Laity: attend, pray at home, commune, be examined** ([§15.8](#s15-8)). Every householder had to bring
children and servants to sermon and catechism. Absentees were counted house by house and fined
(Nassau-Weilburg 1576). The legal minimum for communion was once or twice a year (Hohenlohe
1588), with Luther's "once or four times" as the ideal. Parents were to teach the catechism at
home, and the youth to pray "morning and evening, also before and after meals and at their work"
(Dillenburg 1582).

**7. Church workers: a higher standard** ([§15.8.4](#s15-8-4)). Sextons, schoolmasters and organists were held
to the conduct required of ministers: "like other ministers of the church, of honest and godly
conduct, no drunkards" (Hesse 1566, Moderate Reformed). They were barred from taverns (Hoya
1581) and questioned at visitation about their own communion. The minister's wife, children and
servants were inspected with him.

**8. Schoolmasters: the catechism as primer** ([§15.9](#s15-9)). The schoolmaster taught the catechism, used
it as the reading book, led the boys to sermon and catechism, led the singing, and was visited
four times a year by the pastor (Esslingen 1534, Moderate Reformed; Saxony 1555, 1580). In the
towns schoolmistresses brought the girls (Palatinate 1595, Reformed).

**9. The magistrate: keeper of both tables** ([§15.10](#s15-10)). The Lutheran magistrate was to "uphold both
tables of the Ten Commandments … in maintaining outward discipline" (Mecklenburg 1552). He was
the "defender and nourisher" of churches and schools (Transylvania 1572). In practice he:
- ordered visitation;
- appointed and paid ministers;
- enforced attendance;
- punished what the church could only admonish;
- in the Palatinate (1599, 1608, Reformed), refused citizenship and marriage to those who did
  not know the catechism.

The Reformed limited his office to "the body and temporal goods" (Hanau 1609, Reformed).

**10. Catechesis: how often, how long, and what it required** ([§15.11](#s15-11)).
- **Rhythm:** a weekly Sunday catechism of about half an hour, quarterly fortnight-long series
  (Saxon visitations 1529), a yearly examination in Lent, and house-by-house examinations.
- **Requirement:** the text of the five or six chief parts by heart, and enough understanding to
  "pray and give a fair account of the chief articles" (Saxony 1555).
- **Before first communion:** at Hohenlohe (1578), children of about twelve were taught "every
  day for an hour" from Invocavit to Palm Sunday.

**11. First communion and confirmation: usually one act** ([§15.11.3](#s15-11-3)). Where the orders have
confirmation, the children are "confirmed and admitted to communion for the first time" together
(Hesse 1566, Moderate Reformed). One course of instruction served both. Mansfeld (1580) examined
them publicly the day before, monthly. Lauenburg (1585) confirmed twice a year, and
Hessen-Kassel (1610, Reformed) heard them again after six months. Where there was no rite, as in
Electoral Saxony, examination alone admitted to communion.

**12. Infant communion: acknowledged as ancient, set aside** ([§15.11.6](#s15-11-6)). No order gives the Supper
to infants or argues for it. Four orders name the practice:
- Hesse (1566, Moderate Reformed) and Hohenlohe (1578) grant that infants communed in the time
  of Cyprian and Augustine, but defer the Supper because of 1 Corinthians 11:28 and "the common
  judgment of the first church". Hesse leaves the old custom "in its worth".
- Oldenburg (1573) says that infants cannot examine themselves or discern the Lord's body.
- The Reformed preacher at Markirch (1561) calls it an error of the ancients, who thought that
  the uncommunicated were lost.

Children who died before first communion were buried like adults (Regensburg 1572/1588;
Henneberg 1582). A dying child who knew the catechism might commune before confirmation
(Nassau-Dillenburg 1575, Philippist).

**13. Before marriage: examination, not counselling** (§§[15.11.4](#s15-11-4)–[15.11.5](#s15-11-5)). From the 1560s many orders
refused to proclaim or marry young people who did not know the catechism (Saxony 1580; Hesse
1566, Moderate Reformed; Zweibrücken 1574), "since they are to keep house and get children and
servants". Some married them on a pledge, backed if need be by sureties, to attend the catechism
afterwards (Wied 1616, Reformed). There was no counselling course. What the orders required was:
- an interview some weeks before, on freedom to marry, parents' consent and the catechism
  (Limpurg 1610: three weeks);
- confession and communion before the wedding (Schwäbisch Hall 1615; Freudenthal 1592);
- the public exhortation and wedding sermon on the duties of marriage.

---

### <a id="s15-2"></a>15.2 Scope, sources and method

#### <a id="s15-2-1"></a>15.2.1 Sources and searches

The guide draws on the full text of the Sehling edition in `eko.db`: the church orders,
consistorial and visitation orders, synodal decrees, school and stipend ordinances, and
visitation protocols printed with them. The corpus was searched for the vocabulary of each
question, in High and Low German and Latin spellings:
- **Offices:** *Pfarrer*, *Diaconus*, *Kaplan*, *Superintendent*, *Superattendent*, *Inspector*,
  *Decanus*, *Consistorium*, *Präsident*, *Director*, *Professor*, *facultas theologica*.
- **Training:** *Stipendium*, *Stipendiat*, *Alumnus*, *Probpredigt*, *examen*, *ordinandus*,
  *Synodus*, *Convent*, *censura*, *studieren*, *Bücher*.
- **Laity:** *Hausvater*, *Gesinde*, *daheim*, *Kirchgang*, *Strafe*, *Küster*, *Opfermann*,
  *Schulmeister*, *Schulfrau*.
- **Magistrate:** *Obrigkeit*, *custos utriusque tabulae*, *beide Tafeln*.
- **Catechesis:** *Katechismus*, *Kinderlehre*, *Verhör*, *Examen*, *zum ersten Mal* with
  *Sakrament* or *Nachtmal*, *confirmieren*, and *Katechismus* within a short distance of
  *Braut*, *Eheleute*, *copulieren*, *aufbieten* or *Hochzeit*.
- **Infant communion:** *kinder*, *kindlein*, *unmündig*, *infantes*, *parvuli* and *pueri*
  within a short distance of *Nachtmal*, *Abendmahl*, *Sakrament*, *coena* or *communio*; *prüfe
  sich selbst* and *probet se ipsum* near *Kinder*; *Cyprian*, *Augustin* and *alte Kirche* near
  *Kinder*; *Böhmen*, *Picarden* and *Hussiten*.

Each hit was read in its context. Pages were checked against Sehling's running heads, which
often correct the database's record headings. Among the corrections:
- the Mansfeld agenda quoted is of 1580, though its record is dated 1562;
- the Schwäbisch Hall passages on marriage belong to the revision of 1615, not the order of
  1543;
- the consistory order of 1608 is Ysenburg-Birstein's (Reformed), and the deacons' rule of 1550
  is Breslau's;
- the Palatine passages (Reformed) on probation and convents are from the *Kirchenratsordnung*
  of 1564 and Wenzel Zuleger's report of 1571, though their record is dated 1585.

#### <a id="s15-2-2"></a>15.2.2 What was not found

- **No seminary.** No order founds an institution for training ministers apart from the
  universities, the stipend houses and the Latin and cloister schools. The word *seminarium*
  occurs only in the old sense of a "nursery" of church and state.
- **No vicarage year.** No order prescribes a fixed period of practical training under a pastor
  before ordination. The nearest equivalents are practice preaching ([§15.7.2](#s15-7-2)), the probation as
  deacon ([§15.7.4](#s15-7-4)), and Wittenberg's "some weeks" of instruction ([§15.7.3](#s15-7-3)).
- **No continuing-education requirement in hours or courses.** Continuing study was enforced
  through synods, convents, assigned reading and visitation questions ([§15.7.5](#s15-7-5)).
- **No premarital counselling course.** Instruction before marriage meant an examination in the
  catechism and in the freedom to marry, and often confession and communion. The teaching on
  marriage itself was given publicly in the wedding exhortation and sermon ([§15.11.5](#s15-11-5)).
- **No paedocommunion.** No order gives the Supper to infants or defends the practice, and none
  mentions the Bohemian communion of infants. The orders that name it treat it as an ancient
  custom now set aside ([§15.11.6](#s15-11-6)).
- **No separate confirmation course.** Where confirmation existed it coincided with first
  communion, and one instruction served both ([§15.11.3](#s15-11-3)).
- **No prayer rule for lay church workers.** The lay offices had duties of conduct and
  attendance, not of prayer. The daily office bound schools and convents, not sextons ([§15.8.4](#s15-8-4)).

---

### <a id="s15-3"></a>15.3 Pastors and deacons

#### <a id="s15-3-1"></a>15.3.1 The office in a list

**The visitation questions.** The orders rarely define the pastor's office in the abstract. They
list what the visitors are to ask about, and those lists are the best summary of what was
expected. Strasbourg's order of 1598 puts the whole office in one sentence and then turns to the
minister's life and household. **Strasbourg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1598** (Sehling 20/1, p. 689):

<!-- doc 1344 -->
> Soll derwegen bei der Kirchen Visitation gehandelt werden: 1. Von der Kirchendiener (es seie
> deren an jedem Orth einer oder mehr) offentlichem Ampt und Befelch, Ob sie denselben mit
> gebürendem Fleiß und Trew verrichten, Als mit Predigen, Sacramenta reichen, Catechismum
> halten, Hochzeiten einsegnen und Krancke und Betrübte besuchen und trösten und anderm
> dergleichen, 2. Von ihrem, der Kirchendiener, Leben und Wandel, Auch von ihrer Haußhaltung,
> Weib, Kinder und Gesinde,

Therefore at the visitation of the church there shall be dealt with: 1. The public office and
charge of the ministers of the church (whether there be one or more of them in each place),
whether they perform the same with due diligence and faithfulness, as with preaching, giving the
sacraments, holding the catechism, blessing weddings, and visiting and comforting the sick and
the sorrowful, and other such things; 2. Their life and conduct, the ministers', and also their
housekeeping, wife, children and servants.

The same headings recur everywhere: preaching ([Chapter 11](#ch11)), the
sacraments and the occasional rites
([Chapter 13](#ch13)), the catechism ([§15.11](#s15-11) below), the
sick, and the minister's own life. The daily office laid no breviary obligation on the parish
pastor ([Chapter 10](#ch10), [§10.6.5](#s10-6-5)).

#### <a id="s15-3-2"></a>15.3.2 Study and the pastor's books

**A reading list.** The Saxon General Articles of 1557 name the books every pastor must read:
the Bible, Luther's postil, Melanchthon's *Loci*, and the Augsburg Confession with its Saxon
*Repetition* of 1551. The elector had a copy of the confessions printed for every parish, to
stay in the church's inventory. **Electoral Saxony, *General-Artikel und gemeiner Bericht*,
1557** (Sehling 1, p. 322):

<!-- doc 37 -->
> Sie sollen ihr weib und kind zur zucht und erbarkeit ziehen, aller unehrlichen hantierungen,
> auch wein - oder bierschenkens, kaufmanschaft und dergleichen hendel sich enthalten, auf der
> canzel die leute ex affectu nicht schmehen, ires studii und ambts warten, und sonderlich neben
> der biblia die postillen Lutheri, locos theologicos Philippi lateinisch oder deutsch, die
> augspurgische confession sampt derselben obbemelten repetition sollen sie oft und fleissig
> lesen, und alle ire predigten und lehr auf dieselben confessionen und declarationen gründen
> und richten, damit einerlei form und eintrechtigkeit in der lehr in s. churf. g. landen
> erhalten, und auf die nachkommenden gepflanzt werde

They shall bring up their wife and children in discipline and honesty, abstain from all
dishonest dealings, also from selling wine or beer, from merchandise and such trades, not revile
the people in the pulpit *ex affectu*, wait upon their study and office; and especially, besides
the Bible, they shall read often and diligently Luther's postils, Philip's *Loci theologici* in
Latin or German, [and] the Augsburg Confession together with its aforesaid Repetition, and
ground and direct all their sermons and teaching upon these same confessions and declarations,
that one form and concord in doctrine may be kept in his Electoral Grace's lands and planted for
those that come after.

**Books bought by the parish.** Where a pastor was too poor to buy them, the parish bought them.
Hoya in 1581 orders the churchwardens to provide "a good Wittenberg Bible, Doctor Luther's
postils and catechisms", the parish making up any shortfall, "that such books may be bought for
the church and remain there" (Sehling 6/2, pp. 1140–1141). The pastor's private study was an
item of visitation: the Limpurg visitation order of 1611 asks "what writings and books he
readeth, and what his private studies be", and the visitor is to exhort him to study if he is
found idle (Sehling 16, p. 627). Synods set reading for the year ahead ([§15.7.5](#s15-7-5)).

#### <a id="s15-3-3"></a>15.3.3 Life, household and conduct

**An example to the flock.** The same Saxon articles require ministers and schoolmasters to be
"right and pure in doctrine" and blameless in life, to marry, and to keep out of taverns.
**Electoral Saxony, *General-Artikel und gemeiner Bericht*, 1557** (Sehling 1, p. 322):

<!-- doc 37 -->
> so wollen s. churf. g. das beide kirchen - und schulen - diener vornemblich in der lehre
> richtig und reine sein, auch sonsten in irem leben und wandel sich beide in worten, werken und
> kleidunge erbarlich gegen menniglich, freundlich, züchtig und demütig, und in summa
> allenthalben und in allem christlich und also vorhalten, das sie menniglich, und sonderlich
> ihren schul- und kirchen-kindern nicht anstössig, sondern dermassen mit gutem exempel
> Vorgehen, das die pfar-kinder und sonsten menniglich denselbigen mit lust und frucht
> seliglichen und ane ergernis folgen mügen, hiezu dann vornemblich dienen würde, da sie zu
> vormeidunge menschlicher uppigkeit und heraus folgenden Verdachts sich in den heiligen
> ehestand begeben, […] ires ampts und studirens fleissig abwarteten, saufens, spaciren - gehens
> und anderer ergerlichen leichtfertigkeit, auch aller taberneu und schenk - heuser enthielten

his Electoral Grace will that both ministers of churches and of schools be above all right and
pure in doctrine, and otherwise in their life and conduct, both in words, works and clothing,
behave themselves honestly towards every man, friendly, chastely and humbly, and in sum
everywhere and in all things christianly, and so that they be no stumbling block to any man, and
especially to their school- and church-children, but go before with so good an example that the
parishioners and every man else may follow them blessedly with delight and fruit and without
offence. Whereto it would chiefly serve that they, to avoid human wantonness and the suspicion
that followeth from it, enter into holy matrimony, […] wait diligently upon their office and
study, [and] abstain from drinking, from walking abroad and other offensive frivolity, and from
all taverns and ale-houses.

The articles allow a pastor to sell by the cask the wine or beer of his own glebe or tithe,
"only that they hang out no tavern sign nor set guests to drink in the house"
(Sehling 1, p. 322). Their dress is treated in
[Chapter 14](#ch14), [§14.8](#s14-8).

**The household inspected.** The minister's wife, children and servants were visited with him.
The Württemberg visitation order of 1559 tells the special superintendent to find out "whether
the ministers instruct their children in prayer and the catechism, and keep their boys at school
or teach them themselves at home", and to ask each pastor about the "doctrine, life and
housekeeping" of his colleagues and neighbours "and of their wives and children"
(Sehling 16, p. 387). A Württemberg visitation order of 1547 gives the reason from 1 Timothy 3:
"he that ruleth not his house well, how shall he rule the house of the Lord?"
(Sehling 16, p. 151). The Oldenburg visitation articles of 1609 ask the parish "how the pastor's
wife and children behave themselves towards divine service and live" (Sehling 7/2.1, p. 1192).

#### <a id="s15-3-4"></a>15.3.4 Residence and records

**Residence.** A pastor was not to leave his parish overnight without leave and a substitute.
**Hoya, *Kirchenordnung*, 1581** (Sehling 6/2, p. 1140):

<!-- doc 2065 -->
> Derhalben befehlen wir allen und jeden unsern pfarherrn, schulmeistern und küstern, das sich
> niemand lange von seinem kaspel und ampt, es sey eine oder mehr nacht, ohne nötige ursach
> begebe und habe von unsern verordneten inspectorn ein jeder in seinem eingesetzten ampt
> verlaub genommen und eine tüchtige und wolbekante person aus seiner nachbarschaft in unser
> graffschaft in seinem abwesen gefördert und bestellet.

Therefore we command all and every one of our pastors, schoolmasters and sextons that none
betake himself long from his parish and office, be it one night or more, without needful cause,
and [unless] each have taken leave of our appointed inspectors in his appointed office, and have
procured and appointed a fit and well-known person out of his neighbourhood in our county [to
serve] in his absence.

Marienhafe in East Frisia copied the rule in 1593 (Sehling 7/1, p. 728). In the towns the
deacons needed the pastor's leave, as at Breslau in 1550 and Regensburg in 1556
(Sehling 3, p. 418; 13, p. 443).

**The parish register.** From mid-century the pastor kept registers of baptisms, marriages and
burials, and the visitors inspected them. **Saxony, *Kirchenordnung*, 1580**
(Sehling 1, p. 397):

<!-- doc 44 -->
> Damit man auch gewiss sein möge, das ein jeder pfarrer in seiner kirchen vermög unser ordnung
> die neugetauften kinder, sampt ihrer eltern und paten namen, auf welchen tag sie getauft,
> desgleichen auch der neuen eheleut namen, auf welchen tag sie getrauet und hochzeit gehalten,
> auch welchen tag ein jeder verstorben, verzeichnis und register halte, sol der visitator, so
> oft er visitieret, ihme solches buch, darein es alles ordentlich verzeichnet, vorbringen
> lassen

And that it may be certain that every pastor in his church, according to our order, keepeth a
list and register of the newly baptized children together with their parents' and godparents'
names, on what day they were baptized, likewise of the names of the new married folk, on what
day they were wedded and held their wedding, and also on what day each one died, the visitor, as
often as he visiteth, shall have that same book, wherein all this is orderly written, brought
before him.

The register was to stay with the church and not leave with the pastor or his widow.
Nassau-Weilburg (1576) adds confirmations (Sehling 10, p. 307), and some orders add the
communicants (Kapellendorf 1569, Sehling 1, p. 583). In Pirna (1578) the sexton kept the book,
and at Regensburg (1572) he kept the register of the dead (Sehling 1, p. 645; 13, p. 509).

#### <a id="s15-3-5"></a>15.3.5 Deacons and chaplains

**The assistant ministers.** The *Diaconus* or *Kaplan* was an ordained assistant
([Chapter 16](#ch16), [§16.5.1](#s16-5-1)). His
particular charges were the catechism and the sick. **Electoral Saxony, *Generalia, alle
superintendentes belangende*, 1555** (Sehling 1, p. 315):

<!-- doc 36 -->
> Den catechismum sollen sie der jugent vleissig furtragen, und im leren derselben nit ihre
> kunst und geschicklichkeit beweisen wollen, sundern die kindern lehr dem unverstendigen jungen
> volk ufs aller einfeltigst und immer uf einerlei form und weiss fursagen, und also wider von
> ihnen fordern und examinieren. In besuchung der kranken sollen sie willig und unverdrossen
> sein, und mehr bereit, den armen hierin zu dienen, denn den reichen

They shall diligently set forth the catechism to the youth, and in teaching it not seek to show
their art and skill, but say the children's doctrine before the unlearned young folk in the
simplest way and always in one form and manner, and so require it again of them and examine
[them]. In visiting the sick they shall be willing and unwearied, and readier to serve the poor
herein than the rich.

They were to honour and obey their pastor and superintendent and "not belittle them before the
congregation, nor practise against them, nor stir up factions" (Sehling 1, p. 315). The deacon
was chosen by the pastor together with the council (Sehling 1, p. 323).

---

### <a id="s15-4"></a>15.4 Superintendents and deans

#### <a id="s15-4-1"></a>15.4.1 The name and the office

**One overseer, many names.** The evangelical orders replaced the bishop's oversight with a
superintendent (*Superattendens*, *Inspector*, *Dechant*, *Decanus*, *Propst*). Augsburg in 1537
(Moderate Reformed) justifies the office from the apostolic church and says outright that the
titles are one. **Augsburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1537** (Moderate Reformed; Sehling 12, p. 55):

<!-- doc 338 -->
> derhalb bei den aposteln und hernacher in den kirchen allweg ain oder gar wenig furnemer
> ufseher, furgänger, superattendeten oder bischof, welche namen all ainerlai heischen, in jeder
> gemain verordnet worden send, damit dann nicht alhie durch vil hirten dester ubler gehuetet
> werde […] In suma: sie sollen allerdingen die höchste sorg und fursehung der gemainen Christi
> uf in haben, versehen und versorgen.

therefore among the apostles, and afterwards in the churches, there have always been appointed
in every congregation one or very few chief overseers, leaders, superattendents or bishops,
which names all mean one thing, that here the flock be not the worse kept through many shepherds
[…] In sum: they shall in all things have upon them, oversee and provide the highest care and
provision of the congregation of Christ.

At Augsburg (1537, Moderate Reformed) the office rotated quarterly between the council's
president and the senior provost. In the territories it was a standing office. Its installation
is in [Chapter 13](#ch13), [§13.11.4](#s13-11-4).

#### <a id="s15-4-2"></a>15.4.2 Electoral Saxony, 1555–1557: visitation, synod, report

**The Saxon pattern.** The Saxon General Articles of 1557 set out the superintendent's duties
that most later Lutheran orders follow:
- watch over "the doctrine, life and diligence" of all pastors and church servants in his
  district;
- summon the village pastors once a year, and visit unannounced, to hear their sermons, ask the
  parishioners about their pastor's conduct, examine the youth in the catechism and inspect the
  schools;
- hold a synod every year;
- admonish privately, and report what he cannot mend to the consistory.

**Electoral Saxony, *General-Artikel und gemeiner Bericht*, 1557** (Sehling 1, pp. 320–321):

<!-- doc 37 -->
> Darüber sol ein jeder superattendens nach seiner und der benachbarten pfarherrn gelegenheit
> alle jar zwischen ostern und pfingsten einen synodum halten, und darzu berufen aus den
> stedten, flecken und dörfern alle pastores, so in seine superattendents gehören, und sich
> dorinnen irer lahr und sitten, auch anderer vorfallenden gebrechen erkunden, dieselben in
> besserung richten, insonderheit auch ire relation hören, wie sie ire pfarkinder in examine
> befunden, und was sie sonst vor irrige sachen anzuzeigen haben, und do etwas fürfiele, das er
> nicht vorrichten könte, sol er das an das consistorium, dohin die person und sachen gehörig,
> weisen und gelangen lassen. Do auch der superattendens etwas ungebürlichs oder streflichs von
> einigem pfarherr in seine superattendents gehörig selbst erfaren, oder aber vom lehenherrn,
> oder den eingepfarten erkundigung bekommen hette, sol er denselben in geheim darumb
> ansprechen, und nach gelegenheit der vorbrechunge strafen, mit vorwarnung, do keine besserung
> folgen, und dergleichen klage mehr für ihn kommen würde, das er solches an das consistorium
> gelangen lassen müste

Moreover every superattendent shall, as it suiteth him and the neighbouring pastors, hold a
synod every year between Easter and Whitsun, and call thereto out of the towns, market towns and
villages all the pastors that belong to his superintendency, and therein inquire into their
doctrine and manners and other defects that fall out, and bring the same to amendment; and
especially hear their report, how they have found their parishioners in the examination, and
what other erroneous matters they have to declare. And if anything fell out that he could not
settle, he shall refer it and bring it to the consistory to which the person and matter belong.
And if the superattendent himself have learned of anything unseemly or blameworthy in any pastor
belonging to his superintendency, or have received information of it from the patron or the
parishioners, he shall speak to him about it in secret and rebuke him according to the
circumstances of the offence, with warning that, if no amendment followed and more complaints of
the like came before him, he must bring it before the consistory.

**Other charges.** The superintendent also:
- examined candidates for a parish before sending them to Wittenberg or Leipzig for ordination
  ([§15.7.3](#s15-7-3));
- installed new pastors before the altar and charged both pastor and people (Sehling 1, p. 321);
- saw that no pastor was dismissed without his knowledge (Sehling 1, p. 312);
- settled the widow's year and the parish inventory when a pastor died (Sehling 1, p. 312).

The 1555 *Generalia* add a yearly meeting of all the superintendents of the Electoral circle at
Wittenberg on the Wednesday after Whitsun, where they reported to the pastor of Wittenberg "as
the upper superintendent" (Sehling 1, p. 312). The visitor's travelling costs were refunded on a
weekly account sent to the elector "into his own hands" (Sehling 1, p. 311).

#### <a id="s15-4-3"></a>15.4.3 The superintendent's charge: Grubenhagen, 1600

**An instruction under oath.** The Brunswick consistory's instruction for the superintendent of
Grubenhagen, on which he was sworn in 1600, shows the office at the end of the century: guardian
of doctrine, visitor, and agent of the consistory. **Grubenhagen, *Officium superintendentis
Grubenhagici*, 1600** (Sehling 6/2, p. 1109):

<!-- doc 2058 -->
> 1. Das er sich, dem corpori doctrinae Julio und formulae ooncordiae im gesunden verstande
> durchaus gleichmeißig in thesi et antithesi zu lehren und, das seine untersetzten pfarherrn
> dergleichen thun mugen, vleisiche aufsicht zu haben verpflichte. […] 4. Das er kein dorf oder
> hauß von seiner superintendenz eximiret achte, noch jemands mit seiner befohlnen visitation in
> seinem untergegebenen gezirk praeterire […] 5. Es soll der superintendens keine offentliche
> sunde oder ärgerliche handel den pastoribus und kirchendienern ubersehen

1. That he bind himself to teach in sound understanding, wholly in accord with the *Corpus
   doctrinae Julium* and the Formula of Concord, *in thesi et antithesi*, and to keep diligent
   oversight that the pastors under him may do the like. […] 4. That he hold no village or house
   exempt from his superintendency, nor pass over anyone in his appointed visitation within the
   district put under him […] 5. The superintendent shall overlook no public sin or offensive
   dealing in the pastors and ministers of the church.

He was to change no ceremony without the consistory's ruling, to act always *pro matrimonio* in
marriage cases, and to settle small matters with the district governor rather than "trouble the
consistory lightly" (Sehling 6/2, p. 1109).

#### <a id="s15-4-4"></a>15.4.4 Deans of the Transylvanian chapters

**Elected deans.** Among the Transylvanian Saxons the pastors of each chapter elected their own
dean (*decanus*). **Transylvania, Statutes of the Chapter of Lasseln, 1572**
(Sehling 24, p. 361):

<!-- doc 1692 -->
> Officium decani est ecclesiarum et scholarum sua dioecesis agere inspectorem ac pro virili sua
> parte cavere, ne haereses, schismata morumque vitia pullulent. Deinde publicis invigilare
> commodis atque conventus indicere fratribus non nisi sufficiente aliqua ingenti causa. Ad haec
> defendere bonos ac insontes contra quasvis iniurias intra et extra capitulum ipsis illatas.
> Econtra vero severissime animadvertere in rebelles, ignavos, fucos aut quoquomodo infamiam et
> sibi privatim et toti fraternitati palam creantes.

The office of the dean is to act as inspector of the churches and schools of his diocese, and to
take care to the utmost of his power that heresies, schisms and vices of manners spring not up.
Next, to watch over the common good, and to call the brethren to assembly only for some
sufficient and weighty cause. Besides this, to defend the good and innocent against all wrongs
done them within and without the chapter. But on the other hand to punish most severely the
rebellious, the slothful, the drones, and those who in any way bring disgrace both privately on
themselves and openly on the whole brotherhood.

For his pains each brother paid him one florin a year. The chapter also judged marriage cases,
"which pious magistrates of old, not without weighty counsel, referred to the ecclesiastical
court" (Sehling 24, pp. 361–362).

---

### <a id="s15-5"></a>15.5 Consistories, their presidents and members

#### <a id="s15-5-1"></a>15.5.1 Composition: theologians and jurists

**A mixed court.** The consistory was a standing court of theologians and lawyers under the
prince, for marriage cases, church discipline and the affairs of ministers and church property.
Wittenberg's of 1539 had two theologians and two doctors of law, mostly professors of the
university (Sehling 7/2.2, p. 306, n. 2). Jena's in 1569 was presided over by the superintendent
of Jena, who was to be a doctor of theology. **Saxe-Weimar, *Ordnung und reformation
ecclesiastici consistorii zu Jena*, 1569** (Sehling 1, p. 234):

<!-- doc 24 -->
> Wir ordnen und wollen auch, das in diesem consistorio der superintendens zu Jen, so ein doctor
> theologiae sein soll, praeses sein, und im zween andere theologi, aus den professorn, oder
> kirchendienern, und dann zween geschickte gottsfürchtige juristen, und unser amptman daselbst,
> oder ein ander person vom adel, als assessores zugeordnet werden

We ordain and will also that in this consistory the superintendent of Jena, who shall be a
doctor of theology, be president, and that two other theologians, out of the professors or the
ministers of the church, and then two able, God-fearing jurists, and our district officer there,
or another person of the nobility, be joined to him as assessors.

#### <a id="s15-5-2"></a>15.5.2 The president: prince, nobleman or councillor

**Who presided.** The orders disagree about who should preside:
- **The prince himself.** At Weimar in 1561 Duke Johann Friedrich made himself "the supreme
  president" and meant to attend "in our own princely person", with his brothers deputizing
  (Sehling 1, pp. 230–231).
- **A theologian.** At Jena in 1569 the superintendent presided (above).
- **A nobleman.** Electoral Saxony in 1580 set over its upper consistory at Dresden "an
  understanding, well-qualified [man] of the nobility as president and director of all the
